Title: What's working in B2B GTM in 2026

URL Source: https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/2026-state-of-b2b-gtm-report

Published Time: 2026-10-14T16:50:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Shipping new products used to be the bottleneck for growth. Now the harder part is distributing and monetizing them.

The GTM channels we used to rely on got saturated or started to decline (RIP corporate blogs). Newer channels emerged, including AI search and signal-based plays, although it’s never clear whether we’re early or late to the party.

To understand what’s going on I asked readers: what’s working in go-to-market (GTM) right now?

Maja Voje from [GTM Strategist](https://knowledge.gtmstrategist.com/) and I surveyed 300 software GTM leaders for our second annual [**State of B2B GTM report**](https://stateofb2bgtm.com/). Compared to [last year](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/2025-state-of-b2b-gtm-report) we have a much richer dataset, including a large sample of AI-natives (25% of respondents) and companies with >$50M in ARR (16%). We also have better insight into year-on-year trends: what’s hot, what’s not, and where is GTM heading next.

Today I’ll share my 5 favorite takeaways. The [**40-page PDF report**](https://stateofb2bgtm.com/) is free thanks to support from our amazing GTM partners. (For premium subscribers, keep reading to get your own custom version of the report.)

1.   Founder-led sales persists for longer than you’d expect.

2.   The GTM channel scorecard shows a shift to “anti-AI” channels.

3.   AI search breaks into the mainstream. Don’t treat it like a regular growth channel.

4.   Signals are hot. If only we could agree about which ones.

5.   The new GTM tech stack is Claude Code meets context.

These amazing partners made our research possible:

**PRESENTING PARTNER**

[![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/42971e2d-6d3a-4b1f-a494-6a6408939954/GTM_Banner__1_.png?t=1791727299)](https://ploy.ai/?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=display&utm_campaign=gtm_summit&utm_content=v1_10_14_2026)

Ploy is the marketing platform that turns your website into an always-on growth engine. [**Try it for free.**](https://ploy.ai/?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=display&utm_campaign=gtm_summit&utm_content=v1_10_14_2026)

**GOLD PARTNERS**

![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/e48fd24b-3ce5-430e-881b-2e28e437153d/image.png?t=1791928157)

[**Sumble**](https://sumble.com/?utm_source=maja-state-of-gtm&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=state-of-gtm-2026-oct)→ High precision GTM data + intelligence.

[**Primer**](https://www.sayprimer.com/?utm_source=email&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=stateofb2b-promotion&utm_content=state-of-b2b)→ Target your ICP across LinkedIn, Meta, Google, Reddit, and more — measure performance and know what to do next.

**SILVER PARTNERS**

## Who participated in the 2026 report

It’s important to know exactly where this data comes from before using it to plan your GTM. The survey was run in September 2026. A typical respondent was $1-10M ARR, had an average contract value of $5-50k, based in the US, and selling a product that’s a hybrid of SaaS and AI.

The participants-at-a-glance:

*   **Product type:**Split fairly evenly between AI-native (25% of respondents), SaaS (20%), and hybrids of SaaS and AI (33%). The portion of SaaS-only is down from 41% in last year’s survey. The remainder included services firms and larger enterprises.

*   **ARR:**Mix of early-stage startups with <$1M ARR (32% of respondents), expansion stage startups with $1-10M ARR (35%), growth stage scaleups with $10-50M ARR (18%), and later-stage scaleups with >$50M ARR (16%).

*   **Deal size:**Mostly had an average deal size between $5-50k (49% of respondents) with representation below $5k (21%) and above $50k (30%).

## Insight 1: Founder-led sales persists for longer than you’d expect.

Most B2B companies have a primary GTM motion: a structured, repeatable, and coordinated way to acquire customers that they can rely on consistently.

Last year we asked about 6 GTM motions: inbound, outbound, partners, account-based GTM, product-led growth (PLG) and paid digital. This time around we added founder-led sales, thinking it might be popular among early-stage startups (<$500k ARR).

**It turns out that founder-led sales persists for far longer than we expected.**It’s the leading GTM motion in the survey. It’s the runaway motion up to $1M ARR (44% of respondents) and holds the #2 spot between $1-10M ARR (26% of respondents). It even persists between $10-50M ARR before finally subsiding.

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/45c4f8b3-67df-40c1-82ff-07cbf2252ba2/The_GTM_Motions_in_B2B.png?t=1791741210)

Excluding founder-led sales, deal size makes a big difference for which GTM motions get adopted. Those with smaller deal (<$5k) opt for PLG (35%) or inbound (17%). Large deals (>$50k) go for outbound (31%), inbound (24%), and account-based GTM (19%). The in-betweens settle on inbound (31%) or outbound (25%).

**The takeaway:**Founder-led sales works great in the early days, but growth is likely to slow without a more repeatable GTM. Plant seeds early starting with either inbound or outbound.

## Insight 2: The GTM channel scorecard shows a shift to “anti-AI” channels.

We called 2025 the year of endless channel exploration. Software companies said they had 5 core GTM channels and another 5.5 GTM channel experiments.

Well, the number of core GTM channels crept up again this year to 5.5.

The most common GTM channels were network and introductions (62% say it’s core), SEO (51% say it’s core), and LinkedIn posting by founders and employees (50% say it’s core). The most common experiments were signal-based outbound (50% are experimenting with it) and AI search (41% are experimenting).

Popular doesn’t mean effective, and sometimes GTM channels lose ROI once everyone adopts them. We created the 2026 GTM scorecard to help prioritize where to place your bets.

The shorthand for interpreting this two-by-two:

*   **Tried-and-true:**Upper right (popular and effective)

*   **The next big thing:**Upper left (effective but niche)

*   **Oversaturated:**Lower right (popular but lower ROI)

*   **Figuring it out:**Lower left (niche and lower ROI)

![Image 4](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/bd8e8dd3-beef-4f39-b48d-3d64d7934020/2026_GTM_Scorecard.png?t=1791743319)

**The single best channels were decidedly anti-AI: network and introductions (#1) and intimate events (#2).**

AI search surged into the tried-and-true quadrant for the first time this year after being a figuring it out channel in 2025. SEO made the cut, too, and retained a similar position to last year. The [rise of AI search](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/what-s-working-right-now-in-ai-search) doesn’t mean the immediate death of SEO.

The data looks somewhat different by deal size and ARR scale. That’s available in the [full report](https://stateofb2bgtm.com/).

**The takeaway:**Cold outreach is officially oversaturated, and AI SDRs aren’t living up to the early hype. Lean into your network, intimate events, and LinkedIn instead.

## Insight 3: AI search breaks into the mainstream. Don’t treat it like a regular growth channel.

Last year B2B companies were still experimenting with AI search (AEO). It was [hard to measure](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/how-to-measure-the-impact-of-ai-search-the-right-way) and seemed like SEO 2.0.

Well, that’s clearly changed. AI search is now considered a core GTM channel by 39% of respondents, which is up 11 points from last year.**AEO saw the biggest increase in adoption (by far) of any channel we tested.**

Companies with smaller deal sizes (<$5k) and companies with larger scale (>$50M ARR) are seeing the best results. But the adoption and effectiveness are high across all company types.

If that wasn’t enough, AI search retains the top spot for the channel where respondents plan to increase GTM investments the most.

![Image 5](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/ec67d7b4-ba50-4a27-b13f-5dad81dd05a0/2027_channel_bets.png?t=1791745659)

The first wave of AI search (AEO) was about visibility. The next wave needs to be about influence: are AI tools like ChatGPT saying the right things about your product (and [pricing](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/ai-pricing-visibility-data), for that matter) and to the right people? I’m seeing AI search KPIs getting distributed across just about every marketing function. It’s a brand KPI, content KPI, growth KPI, product marketing KPI, and exec-level KPI.

Other observations:

*   I hope you’re hungry because dinners are on the menu in 2027, brought to you by more mature companies (>$10M ARR).

*   Early-stage founders want to become LinkedIn influencers.

*   Cold calling fell to the bottom of the list. Hear me out on this one: will calling be less crowded (and perhaps more effective)?

**The takeaway:**You already know AI is talking about your product and probably tracking AI visibility. The next frontier is [measuring the full impact](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/how-to-measure-the-impact-of-ai-search-the-right-way) of AI search so you can improve performance.

Thanks for reading Growth Unhinged! To receive new posts and support my work, please subscribe or share this post.

## Insight 4: Signals are hot. If only we could agree about which ones.

Signals might be the buzziest buzzword in GTM right now. Combining first-party and third-party data sources helps tell us who’s ready to buy, when to reach them, and how to persuade them. These signals can be used across outbound campaigns, [LinkedIn ads](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/linkedin-ad-playbook), AE outreach, you name it.

**Yet there are a near-infinite number of signals. Nobody seems to agree about which matter and which are a waste of effort.** Companies remain stuck in experimentation mode just like last year.

This year we asked which signals get acted on by GTM teams. It’s mostly content engagement (52% of respondents), website visits (42%), and product usage (40%). Content engagement and website visits are popular across all deal sizes whereas product usage is more widely acted on among those with <$5k ACV.

These signals aren’t exactly novel, although there is better tech for de-anonymizing website visitors or enriching personal emails.

![Image 6](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/99e7f5e5-7f95-4def-970e-faf94f6b3788/2026_State_of_GTM_-_Signals.png?t=1791814543)

There’s far less maturity around third-party signals like social activity (30% of respondents), champion movements (28%), hiring activity (25%), leadership changes (24%), or company events (17%). Tech changes barely register (14%), yet might be the clearest evidence that a company is refreshing their stack.

Interestingly, larger companies aren’t much more mature compared to companies with $1-10M ARR with one exception: they’re far more eager adopters of 3rd party intent data.

I suspect companies are overwhelmed by all the noise, although signals are a [great use case for AI agents](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/the-best-ai-native-gtm-plays-you-re-not-running). Agents could scan your target list continuously, notice multiple signals stack for the same account, and then proactively surface which plays to run.

**The takeaway:**If you’re new to signals, there are four places I’d start:

*   Tracking job changes from existing champions and power users

*   Reactivating closed-lost deals based on leadership or tech changes

*   De-anonymizing website visitors who’ve viewed high-value pages and then targeting their buying groups with digital ads

*   Turning product users into enterprise pipeline

## Insight 5: The new GTM tech stack is Claude Code meets context.

Last year we wrote that while there’s been a proliferation of next-gen GTM tools, only one (ChatGPT) was having a breakout impact. ChatGPT was rated the #1 most impactful GTM tool and the #5 must-try GTM tool.

**Fast forward a year:**[**Claude reigns supreme**](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/2026-claude-code-gtm-report)**and the battle isn’t even close.**Claude jumped from #4 to #1 most impactful GTM tool. It was mentioned by 110 survey participants, which is more than three times as many as the next closest vendor. (Claude Code was the most popular Claude product, indicating that GTM practitioners are getting way more technical.)

![Image 7](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/510fe23e-1dfa-471c-897c-29992930194a/2026_GTM_tech_rankings__improved_readability.png?t=1791816420)

Clay (#2) and HubSpot (#3) were the other most-impactful GTM tools. They swapped places compared to last year. Salesforce jumped into the #5 spot after being out of the top 10 in 2025.

What stood out to me the most was the ‘must try’ GTM tools. 7 of the top 10 ‘must try’ tools weren’t on the list last year! That’s pretty wild. Notable examples are Grok Bot, Profound (which hit a $1.8B valuation in September), Monaco, Common Room (acquired by Zoom), Ploy, and Cursor.

Zooming out, I’d summarize the tech trends as AI-first GTM meets context layers meets signals.

**The takeaway:**Claude Code is now a required skill for GTM teams (here’s a great [case study](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/how-to-use-claude-code-as-a-gtm-leader) from Fin), and GitHub is [replacing the resume](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/why-every-marketer-needs-a-github) as a way to show off AI builds. Welcome to GTM in 2026.

## What comes next in GTM

There are two ways to win right now: being exceptional at relationships and being exceptional at AI. Both ends of the barbell are working. But beware of the space in between.

In a perfect world, AI helps GTM teams get better at what AI can’t replace:

*   Signals can tell us who’s most likely to buy.

*   Highly targeted ads warm prospects up.

*   AI agents accelerate account research.

*   Networking and introductions help us earn the initial meeting.

*   Intimate in-person dinners build trust and seal the deal.

Looking ahead, we believe the next battleground will be positioning and messaging. These softer elements of GTM have been ignored or underappreciated. The result is that every company sounds the same, and customers are tuning out. Being great at AI won’t matter if the pitch falls on deaf ears.

[Bryant Chou](https://www.linkedin.com/in/bryantchou/?isSelfProfile=false), co-founder of [Ploy](https://ploy.ai/?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=display&utm_campaign=gtm_summit&utm_content=v1_10_14_2026), summed this up well in his reaction to the report:

❝

"If you feel like your messaging isn't resonating, you're not speaking to enough customers. The voice of your customer is your messaging. **Customer marketing should be leading your GTM strategy, from positioning down to content pieces that feed every stage of the funnel across every channel.**"

Bryant Chou, co-founder of Ploy

Here’s to another great year in GTM!

Title: CitizenLab Details New Spyware Triggered By Online Advertising

URL Source: https://www.engadget.com/2287417/citizenlab-details-new-spyware-triggered-by-online-advertising/

Published Time: 2026-10-15T12:50:29+00:00

Markdown Content:
It requires 'no interaction' from victims to infect devices.

![Image 1: stock image showing a blue eye made out of zeros and ones](https://www.engadget.com/img/gallery/citizenlab-details-new-spyware-triggered-by-online-advertising/intro-1792068524.jpg)
Vaselena/Getty Images

A new type of [spyware](https://www.engadget.com/2254646/android-phone-how-to-find-remove-spyware/) dubbed "AdFection" is infecting phones and computers via global online advertising networks, according to a new report from [Citizen Lab](https://citizenlab.ca/research/how-discover-tech-turned-targeted-ads-into-a-pipeline-for-spyware/). The attack is unique in that it can infect devices just by showing an ad, with no need for the victim to click on a link or file. The researchers said that AdFection is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads.

The ad-infiltrating technology was reportedly developed by Israeli company called Discover-Tech. Researchers said it has been used to target journalists and staff at the Al Jazeera news network, along with officials and employees at organizations including NATO, the European Commission, NVIDIA and Arm.

"Discover-Tech has leveraged the advertising ecosystem for years to turn trusted websites and popular apps into a zero-click spyware delivery platform," Citizen Lab senior researcher Bill Marczak told _[The Financial Times](https://www.ft.com/content/b857f1ed-8af6-4d64-b059-912afee1c075?syn-25a6b1a6=1)_.Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm but instead serves as a "bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem," Citizen Lab's report states

Google was among the major ad platforms targeted by the spyware, but it has now suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list. "Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies,"the company said in a statement.

Targeted online advertising is a highly desirable medium to spread malware because it's prevalent on the web globally. It works though an automated real-time bidding auction system that lets advertisers compete to show ads to specific internet users. Discover-Tech's software used the system instead to profile and de-anonymize such users before targeting them with spyware, the report states. Victims were then sent malicious malware code buried in innocent-looking ads.

Discover-Tech reportedly displayed 442 million ads on more than 120,000 websites, including the _BBC_ and _New York Times_, along with mobile apps like Duolingo, Badoo and Grindr. The ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure and national cyber agencies. Citizen Lab researchers found login records on Discover-Tech's site, including details belonging to employees of the spyware maker Candiru.

The discovery is "surely just the tip of the iceberg," Marczak said in the blog post."If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it's time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether." Discover-Tech and other players in the scheme have yet to comment.

kept.heading: HOW TO PITCH LOCAL NEWSROOMS IN THE US (9 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Local news pitches are more effective when they target the right journalist, demonstrate a clear community impact, and provide everything needed to produce the story. Local newsrooms have declined by 81% since 2002, making relevant, ready-to-use pitches especially important. Start by reviewing journalists' recent coverage, then contact assignment editors at TV stations or editors at print and digital outlets when appropriate. Tailor pitches to the format: print needs a clear story and supporting data, TV needs visuals and local people to interview, and radio needs an available guest who can speak. Include a timely local angle, relevant data, quotes, visuals, and event details, and send the pitch before the newsroom's morning planning meeting.

Title: How to Pitch Local Newsrooms in the US (Your Definitive 2026 Guide)

URL Source: https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/how-to-pitch-local-newsrooms/

Published Time: 2026-10-14T18:23:15+00:00

Markdown Content:
*   **Start with the most relevant reporter.** Review their recent coverage, then try the assignment editor for TV or an editor for print and digital outlets.
*   **Make the local connection clear.** Show how your story affects the community, and include local people who can bring it to life.
*   **Match your pitch to the format.**Print needs a clear story and supporting data; TV needs visuals and on-camera guests; radio needs someone who can talk.
*   **Give journalists everything they need upfront.**Include data, quotes, visuals, event details, and expert availability to reduce back-and-forth.
*   **Time your pitch around the newsroom.** Aim to arrive before the morning planning meeting in their time zone, and hold off when major breaking news dominates coverage.

Local newsrooms in the US have been shrinking.

A new study from [Local Journalist Index](https://localjournalistindex.com/) shows 7.8 local journalists per 100k residents in 2026, down 81% from 40 per 100,000 in 2002.

As newsrooms cut staff, the remaining journalists are overloaded, and our research shows [they are outnumbered by PR pros](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/journalists-jobs-in-the-us/) at least two-to-one.

So, pitching to these newsrooms requires a different approach than pitching a national publication or a niche publication like TechCrunch.

In this post, I’ll break down how US local newsrooms operate and how to pitch them, drawing on what I’ve learned from interviewing 100+ podcast guests, data from millions of BuzzStream emails, and 10+ years of pitching experience.

## How Local Newsrooms Work

To start, let’s talk about how local newsrooms work, because they aren’t the same as national newsrooms, and not every local newsroom is set up the same way.

The biggest split is between **broadcast** newsrooms (TV stations and their websites) and **non-broadcast** newsrooms (newspapers and digital-only local sites).

Who does what, and who you should pitch, differs significantly in each.

### Broadcast newsrooms (TV stations)

Every TV broadcast newsroom, like the one behind Connecticut’s local [Fox61](https://www.fox61.com/), revolves around the **assignment desk.**

[Mike Fahey](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mifahey), founder of [Fahey Communications](https://www.faheycomm.com/) and a former newsroom producer and news director, called them the gatekeepers.

In our [podcast episode](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/newsrooms-with-mike-fahey/), he told me:

“They’re the ones that are the hub of knowledge. They’re listening to scanners, monitoring the Internet, monitoring emails… they’re also setting the agenda for the day.”

From there, they pick stories in planning meetings, and most newsrooms hold several a day.

Then they assign stories to reporters.

But reporters work different shifts, and each one has a different target.

Every newsroom is different, but here’s how Mike explained his experience at local outlets in Boston and Baltimore:

| Shift | When they start (per Mike) | What Mike says about them |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Morning | ~3 a.m. | “Not a lot of morning reporters are doing a lot of enterprise reporting*.” |
| Day side | Between 9 and 10 a.m. | Where “the bulk of your enterprise reporting” comes from. It’s when officials speak, and news conferences happen. |
| Night side | Between 2 and 3 p.m. | They cover the day’s news and breaking stories. But Mike will pitch a self-contained feature at 3 p.m. to try to get it on the 6 p.m. news. |

(***Note:** “Enterprise reporting” is when a journalist brings their own stories to the table rather than using external news like press releases.)

Again, that’s not a universal schedule.

And remember, a station’s website (like fox61.com) is still part of a broadcast newsroom.

Non-broadcast might look a bit different.

### Non-broadcast newsrooms (newspapers and digital-only sites)

Non-broadcast newsrooms, like Nashville’s daily paper, [The Tennessean](https://www.tennessean.com/), mostly have editors and reporters.

Reporters who get pitches still typically need to “pitch” their stories to an editor who will have the final say.

[Collin Czarnecki](https://www.linkedin.com/in/collinczarnecki), founder of [Noble](https://thisisnoble.co/) and a former Patch editor, has worked on both sides.

[In our podcast](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/local-news-podcast/), he said that some sites are so small they are essentially a “one-man band operation,” where the editor is also the reporter.

That’s a great segue into our next section on figuring out exactly who to pitch at a local newsroom.

## Who to Pitch in Local Newsrooms

Always aim to pitch the **most relevant reporter first,** no matter the newsroom.

[Finding relevant reporters and journalists](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/how-to-find-journalists/) usually means reviewing their last 10-20 articles and gauging how close they are to what you are pitching.

I call this the [F.I.T.](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/journalist-fit/) check (matching format, industry, and timing).

But who comes _next_ depends on what kind of newsroom you’re pitching.

### At a broadcast station

**The assignment editor is second on the list, sometimes first,**depending on who you ask.

[Nicole DeLeon](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nicoleldeleon), Founder at North Star Inbound, ranked the assignment editor first for local TV, calling them “the newsroom’s center (literally and figuratively).”

Mike called the assignment editor “the person who’s gonna like give your story to the masses if you can’t reach them otherwise.”

![Image 1: samantha perelli bio page](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/samantha-perelli-bio-page.png)

On the flip side, Collin told me he uses assignment desk and tip line contacts “sparingly,” because depending on the newsroom, that pitch “might be going to everyone.”

I’d judge based on the _kind_ of content you are pitching.

If your pitch is hyper specific to a category like local sports or a restaurant opening, try to find the reporter covering those.

But if it is data that impacts the whole city, that might warrant an email to the assignment desk.

Titles rarely tell you who works mornings or nights.

Mike searches bios for terms like “nightside” and “morning,” because “it may pop up in their bio.”

For instance, Christian Colon of [WFSB.com](http://wfsb.com/) lists his job title as a reporter. Only in his bio do we see that he is nightside.

![Image 2: christian colon bio page showing nightside stories](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/christian-colon-bio-page-showing-nightside-stories.png)

Collin says he excludes news directors and newsroom directors entirely because they typically manage the newsroom rather than make decisions on stories.

### At a non-broadcast outlet (newspapers and digital-only sites)

After a reporter, **editors are next in line.**

But in certain scenarios, “the smaller the site, the higher up you can go,” he agreed.

At a one-person operation, the editor _is_ the reporter.

You can usually get a sense of the size from the About or Meet the Staff page.

![Image 3: meet the team page on fox61](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/meet-the-team-page-on-fox61.png)

I’ll get into this more in the next section.

For small radio stations, you might be better off pitching the host directly. Otherwise, look for the producer.

## How to Build Your List

Here’s a step-by-step guide to building your local list.

### 1. Map the market

Start with the core outlets in your target city.

First, identify print or digital newspapers, then move to the TV affiliates (typically NBC, CBS, ABC, FOX).

Then you can dig into the secondary local sites like Patch or local newsletter sites like [6AM City.](https://6amcity.com/)

AI is typically very helpful at this these days:

![Image 4: philadelphia local news sites google search](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/philadelphia-local-news-sites-google-search.png)

And don’t sleep on radio.

Collin pointed out that [iHeart](https://www.iheart.com/) has stations all over the country, so a city ranking that includes several iHeart markets can get picked up in more than one of them.

Plus, those stations have websites, so a radio pitch can still turn into online coverage.

### 2. Size up the newsroom

Typically, a newsroom will correlate with the population in a given area. Densely populated metro cities like New York City or Los Angeles need more reporters than a random Midwestern city.

But before pitching an outlet for the first time, check the About or Staff page.

Here is [CT Examiner](https://ctexaminer.com/)’s staff page with 14 writers.

![Image 5: CTExaminer staff page shows 14 writers](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ctexaminer-staff-page-shows-14-writers.png)

Smaller still is Westport, [CT’s Westport Journal](https://westportjournal.com/), which lists just seven staff:

![Image 6: westport journal shows 7 staff](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/westport-journal-shows-7-staff.png)

For context, [NYC’s Fox5 team](https://www.fox5ny.com/team) page lists 30+ people, not including editors and other non-personality staff:

![Image 7: fox5 meet the team page shows 30+ people](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/fox5-meet-the-team-page-shows-30-people.png)

Often, smaller cities or counties are lumped into a larger metro news station’s category.

My hometown, Haddon Township, NJ, for instance, has a category section on a larger outlet on Philadelphia’s [6ABC Action News](https://6abc.com/) site:

![Image 8: 6abc action news haddon township category page](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/6abc-action-news-haddon-township-category-page.png)

When in doubt, look to see who authors the stories most relevant to your target location.

### 3. Find journalists who have covered similar topics

Start hyper-focused based on articles the journalist or reporter has already written.

For most PRs, this is the step that’s slipping. In our 2026 report, only **about 56% of PRs always review a journalist’s recent articles** before pitching, down about 8% from last year.

If you are pitching a survey, find other reporters who have covered similar surveys in the same industry.

Do that by doing a site:search for similar keywords.

For instance, if I’m looking to get a client’s NJ-based restaurant included in a best X restaurant roundup post, I’d search for site: [www.nj.com](http://www.nj.com/) “best restaurants”.

![Image 9: site search for nj.com best restaurants](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/site-search-for-nj-com-best-restaurants.png)

Then I’m clicking into them and checking the authors:

![Image 10: nj.com page pointing to journalist jeremy schneider](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/nj-com-page-pointing-to-journalist-jeremy-schneider.png)

Both [Jeremy](https://www.nj.com/staff/jeremyschneider/) and [Stephanie’s](https://www.nj.com/staff/srizzolo/) author pages show their bios and the fact that they’ve recently covered similar listicle-type stories:

![Image 11: stephani rizzolo author bio showing her existing content](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stephani-rizzolo-author-bio-showing-her-existing-content.png)

This process can be very time-consuming (which is why so many people skip it), but it’s the only way to cut through the noise.

[We built [ListIQ](https://www.buzzstream.com/listiq/) to cut that time down.

It turns a Google News search into a media list in Google Sheets, with emails, bios, recent articles, and whether the journalist is still active at the outlet.]

Next, let’s get into the actual pitch process.

## How to Write Your Pitch

Each type of local outlet needs slightly different information.

Here’s what my guests told me works for each:

| Format | What they need | How to write it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local print/digital | A ready-to-run story with data | Collin writes it “in the style of a news story” so a short-staffed journalist could “pretty much just really pull this” without many changes. Not a full press release. |
| Local TV | Visuals, an on-camera guest, graphics | Collin reads his TV pitches in “the voice of a news anchor” to see if it plays. |
| Local morning shows | Fun visuals for the teaser, interviews for the main segment | Offer hands-on segments for a reporter. |
| Radio | A host or guest who can talk | Collin pitches the host at smaller stations. |

Going a bit deeper, here are some tips for crafting the pitches.

### Give them what they need to write the article

Local journalists typically need more information than nationals because they are so time-poor.

So, when you write a pitch, include everything they need to write the article without emailing you.

**If it’s a data-based pitch,** give them access to the data.

**If it’s commentary,** give them the actual comments. Or, if you are syncing up with a journalist, share times your expert will be available so they can schedule, rather than leaving the ball in their court.

**If it’s an event**, give them the who, what, where, when.

Check out our post with several [media pitch examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/) for some real templates.

### Match the subject line

Journalist inboxes are notoriously overloaded.

Typically, we recommend matching the subject line to a journalist’s headline style.

Go to their author page and look at how they write their pitches.

If I were pitching [Kelsey Gibbs from News Channel 5 Nashvill](https://www.newschannel5.com/about-us/kelsey-gibbs)e, I’d notice she writes headlines with a subject + verb.

*   Nashville travelers leave…
*   Nashville property owner sells…
*   Federal judge dismisses…

(I’d also be sure to say Nashville in my subject line.)

![Image 12: recent stories from kelsey gibbs showing many references to nashville](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/recent-stories-from-kelsey-gibbs-showing-many-references-to-nashville.png)

You can also judge by the homepage.

If most of the homepage is comprised of a single story (like the storm in the screenshot below), that’s usually a signal to hold off on pitching.

![Image 13: homepage of a kansas city news site showing storm coverage](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/homepage-of-a-kansas-city-news-site-showing-storm-coverage.png)

Journalists at local news outlets are typically pulled into covering different beats on these occasions as well, leaving no time to cover their own beats.

## What Makes a Story Work Locally

The best way to understand what works in local markets is to watch, read, and listen.

Collin told me he keeps a streaming app with local Fox affiliates running in the background every morning to learn “not only what they’re talking about, but how they’re talking about it.”

In many markets, breaking news eats everything, and it can get crowded fast.

So your story has to earn its spot. Here’s what helps.

### A real local angle

Some stories, like local events or restaurant openings, are enough to satisfy a local community.

But if you are trying to pitch a data study, for instance, it needs to impact the location you are pitching.

[City index studies](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/city-study/) became a strategy because they highlight a city as the “best” at something, giving the local news something to brag about.

Ask: how does my story or pitch impact the local community?

Traffic reports, shootings, car crashes, and weather dominate local news stations because they clearly impact the local community.

Remember, local newsrooms have traffic and viewership goals, just like your own sites or clients.

### Give it a local face

Can you get local people involved?

If your event is just a salesperson demoing a product, that’s not much of a draw.

But a local family or local chef who uses it and can talk about it?

Here is a story announcing Girl Scout Cookies’ new Exploremores cookie on [Michigan news station WLUC:](https://www.uppermichiganssource.com/2026/01/15/girl-scout-cookie-season-is-here-along-with-new-cookie/)

![Image 14: girl scout cookie season is here - along with a new cookie](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/girl-scout-cookie-season-is-here-along-with-a-new-cookie.png)

The story focused only on the cookie and its release, which, to some, might be the news.

But for Atlanta-based news outlet [Atlanta Journal-Constitution](https://www.ajc.com/arts-entertainment/2026/03/meet-the-metro-atlanta-girl-scouts-featured-on-new-exploremores-cookie-box/), the story features the girls on the box because they are based in the Atlanta area.

![Image 15: meet the metro atlanta girl scouts featured on new exploremores cookie box](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/meet-the-metro-atlanta-girl-scouts-featured-on-new-exploremores-cookie-box.png)

That’s an example of taking a general news story and localizing it.

### Something to show (for TV)

Put yourself in a producer’s shoes.

They need video, graphics, and human beings.

The Girl Scout cookie girls in Atlanta are a perfect example.

But it doesn’t always have to be humans.

I once did a survey to see if people from different cities could spot their own skyline. It got TV coverage because it was a very visual story.

![Image 16: houston skyline stands out among big cities according to survey](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/houston-skyline-stands-out-among-big-cities-according-to-survey.png)

You can even go deeper.

If you want to pitch a story that might get local TV coverage, think about how it looks in the background of a reporter on the scene.

Is there construction happening? Is there a demonstration?

Here’s a story about a [local Ninja Academy opening in LA](https://www.foxla.com/video/1494999) on Fox11:

![Image 17: fox11 la lost angeles ninja academy opening this weekend](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/fox11-la-lost-angeles-ninja-academy-opening-this-weekend.png)

The story went to the scene and showed them actually doing acrobatics.

The local host even got in on the action and did some activities on the mats.

Here’s another where they show off how See’s Candy is made at a [San Francisco candy shop](https://abc7news.com/post/take-a-look-inside-sees-candies-in-south-sf/5152279/) to showcase a holiday release:

![Image 18: see's candies factory in south san francisco cranks up for christmas](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/sees-candies-factory-in-south-san-francisco-cranks-up-for-christmas.png)

These all make a local story something worth covering because they have a strong visual element.

### A timely hook (a real one)

I’ve explained that every pitch should answer “ [why now?](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/why-now/)”

If you can answer that, you put yourself in the mind of an assignment editor.

Going back to my podcast conversation with Mike, he told me that Boston news doesn’t cover restaurant openings.

But one of his clients named his restaurant after his great-grandmother and filmed his mom finding out. Then, he released it on Mother’s Day, and every station in Boston ran it.

![Image 19: cambridges new italian restaurant dessert lounge honors owners female idols](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/cambridges-new-italian-restaurant-dessert-lounge-honors-owners-female-idols.png)

That’s a hook with a real timely connection.

## Think Like the Producer

One idea kept coming up in all of my conversations: think like the person on the other end. Collin calls it having a “newsroom mentality.”

Mike said it best when he talked about his restaurant client: “You have to always be thinking like a producer.”

Local newsrooms are short-staffed and moving fast.

If you make their job easier with the right reporter, a real local angle, something to show, and the right timing, they’re one of the best PR opportunities.

So, pick one city. Build a tight list. Pitch it before the morning meeting.

Good luck!

![Image 20: Vince Nero](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/c843c1c17ddb1c976c95d49abddc1fd02d85c5172bedebe72c33534bb477acee?s=200&d=mm&r=g)

## Vince Nero

Vince is the Director of Content Marketing at Buzzstream. He thinks content marketers should solve for users, not just Google. He also loves finding creative content online. His previous work includes content marketing agency Siege Media for six years, Homebuyer.com, and The Grit Group. Outside of work, you can catch Vince running, playing with his 2 kids, enjoying some video games, or watching Phillies baseball.

Title: Pinterest Business

URL Source: https://business.pinterest.com/en-au/blog/design-the-exit/?_sp=7b571d78-3f73-49e3-ad3e-a4deb121e1f1.1792018446862

Markdown Content:
**40% of Gen Z say that they wish social media had never been invented.**1 This is the generation that grew up online, yet they’re bricking their phones to avoid doomscrolling and rediscovering the joys of IRL. In fact, 63% of Gen Z adults now intentionally unplug—the highest rate of any generation.2 That’s a shift that marketers can’t afford to ignore.

These signals point to a broader shift: people still want inspiration and ideas, but they want them to lead somewhere real. It’s not just about switching off phones, but about using them to live a more meaningful life. The problem is, most online experiences aren’t built for that. They’re built to keep people scrolling.

#### When people are passively scrolling, ads don’t land

Research shows that 44% of the time, when people go online, they get sucked into scrolling and end up somewhere they didn’t intend to be.6 At Pinterest, we have a name for this: the loop.

When people are stuck in the loop, passively scrolling, they’re browsing a continuous feed without a clear goal or time limit. And in this context, ads don’t land—they become part of the scroll, and are more likely to be ignored than acted upon.6

But when people are in a more intentional mode online, they’re using technology to help them take action and make decisions in their real lives. In action mode, brands are less likely to be ignored, and more likely to be purchased, trusted and remembered.6

In a world full of infinite choice and shrinking attention, where AI largely decides what gets surfaced and what gets skipped, reach and receptivity are not the same thing. And while capturing attention is still part of your job as a marketer, connecting with people in action-oriented moments is how you move from being seen to being wanted.

#### So what do you do, as a marketer?

Don’t reinforce the loop. **Design the exit.**

Instead of asking, ‘How do I capture attention?’, ask, ‘How do I ignite intention?’ Help people to find what they need, quickly and confidently, and get them back to the business of living.

Pinterest is where this already happens, by design. We’ve engineered our platform for time well spent. Meaning, instead of building to keep people scrolling, we’re building for the person: what they want to find, what they need to feel and what they’re actually trying to do. And that’s why Gen Z is our largest, fastest-growing demographic, making up over half of our user base.7

We believe that designing the exit can be applied broadly—across your whole marketing strategy and across platforms. It comes down to three key principles:

#### **1. Open the door**

Show that your brand makes a fuller life possible. Make the hero your audience’s world, not your product or service. Your value lies in helping them to see a vivid, specific version of their life that your brand can unlock. It’s not just about selling your product, but about opening possibilities.

Travel inspiration often lives in the gap between ‘some day’ and ‘book it’—and for many people, that gap can feel enormous. Working with Pinterest, Virgin Australia created a series of premium travel video ads designed to spark the imagination and close that distance.

Collage-style visuals helped people to feel the arrival before they’d even left. Even the CTA was ‘Live it’, rather than ‘Book it’. Those two words turned a transaction into an experience worth stepping into.

#### **2. Ignite their intention**

If opening the door is inspiring your audience with possibilities, igniting intention is about helping them get to a decision. This is the messy middle of the funnel and the toughest part of a campaign to land. You can win this phase of the journey by helping people to see how your products or services offer a concrete path to realising their vision.

So instead of vague inspiration, give them personalised options, guidance and next steps so they can not only picture the real-world moment that you’ve unlocked, but also see exactly how to get there. The more specific the better: the exact recipe and shopping list, the full outfit with links, the step-by-step room plan.

#### **3. Set them free**

Lastly, set them free. This is where advertisers need to be brave. Once people have found what they’re looking for, let them go. Don’t trap people in the experience. Let your brand do its job, and then send them back into their life having found what they were looking for.

Starbucks Mexico did this ahead of the 2025 festive season. They reframed their café as the place where festive connection actually happens—and then built something to make it real. They created an add-to-calendar Pin extension with a pre-filled invitation, ready to send to a friend or family member, with a time and a place already set. Rather than reward the loop, Starbucks created a clear pathway out of it.

#### Be a bridge to something real

Open the door, ignite their intention and set them free. That’s what it means to design the exit.

More than ever, people want their time online to mean something and to be in service of the lives that they’re actually trying to live. This shift isn’t about wanting less from technology—it’s about wanting more from it. More relevance, more utility and a path to the things that actually matter.

For marketers, this means reaching people ready for action, not distraction, and Pinterest is the platform to do it. 640 million people come to Pinterest every month 8 to find what they’re looking for, then get back to their lives. That’s what we’ve always been about, and it’s why Pinterest is seen as the most action-oriented social platform, with 69% of monthly users saying that Pinterest leads to real-world decisions, big and small.6 We’re a platform that moves people towards a life they love, and your brand can be the bridge to make it real.

Find out how your brand can fuel a life, not just fill a feed, on Pinterest.
