Title: The Art of Brand Merch

URL Source: https://fatemaraja.substack.com/p/the-art-of-brand-merch

Published Time: 2026-10-15T09:48:05+00:00

Markdown Content:
A few weeks ago I came home to Goa after a summer in Berlin, just in time for my end-of-monsoon clear-out. It is a small ritual. Anything I haven’t used in a year goes into a donation box, or to a friend I know will love it more than I did.

This year, a lot of what went into that box was brand merch.

One of the perks of my job, writing and talking about consumer brands, is that brands send me lovely things. Usually it is their product, and usually the product is good. I use it, and sometimes I buy it again. Tucked in beside it is the merch, and the merch is what ends up in the box. A T-shirt with a company’s logo stretched across the chest. A water bottle with a wordmark I won’t carry anywhere.

I can tell how much thought went into where the logo should sit and what the slogan should say. Far less went into whether anyone would use the thing, or why they would want to walk around with a company’s name across their chest.

I’m not saying brand merch is a waste. Quite the opposite. Made with care, merch is marketing that invites people into a brand’s world, and a few pieces in my wardrobe prove it.

The cap I wear most comes from alag, a small café in Siolim, Goa, that opened in 2023 and calls itself a home for coffee, creativity and conversation ([alag](https://village.ai/company/alag-co)). The obvious move for a café is a mug, a tote, a bag of beans with the logo on it. alag designed for the place it lives in instead: caps and tank tops cut for Goa’s heat and humidity. More than a year on, the cap is still the one I reach for.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jPBP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4c9e7e2f-f150-45e3-8a06-f591744bc76f_1634x656.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jPBP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4c9e7e2f-f150-45e3-8a06-f591744bc76f_1634x656.png)

It is beautifully made, for a start. The bigger reason I wear it is what it says about me. It says I know the café with great coffee that many people are still discovering. It says I like what alag stands for: slow mornings, good coffee, a creative life that isn’t for everyone. It says I choose carefully. Anyone who recognises the cap reads all of that in a second, in whichever city I wear it, and anyone who doesn’t is left a little curious. Either way, the cap is working. A good piece of merch carries a whole world in a few square inches of cotton, and lets the wearer take that world wherever they go.

I’m not unusual in this. Most of us are curating who we are: the books on the shelf, the café we photograph, the bag on our shoulder. Each is a small piece of evidence for the person we would like to be taken for. Nobody wears merch to promote a company. People wear it to say something about themselves, and they will carry your name only if it helps them say it.

So the useful question for a brand is who its customer wants to be, and whether the thing it is making helps them get there. Visibility follows from that.

This matters more now than it did ten years ago. Mainstream culture has split into thousands of small rooms: run clubs, natural wine bars, F1 fans who started watching on Netflix, the regulars of one bakery. Each room needs ways to recognise its own people on the street. Meanwhile, feeds are crowded and ads are easy to scroll past. A tote on a stranger’s shoulder is media a real person chose to carry, and no paid placement can buy that.

Most brands have caught on, so they make some merch. The trouble is that they all make the same things: a tote, a T-shirt, a cap, a notebook with the logo on it (and many of those logos need a serious redesign). A skincare label and a fintech app end up with identical merch tables.

A good T-shirt with a slogan is still a T-shirt with a slogan, and a logo on a water bottle is still a logo on a water bottle. Both ask the customer to carry the brand’s message without giving them a reason to. Established luxury houses and a handful of very successful brands can get away with a logo, because their logo already means something. OpenAI’s Supply Co. is a good example ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/supply/shop/)).

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wF-k!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F97def28d-41aa-4bb1-b74e-3ddc13b52a8e_742x682.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wF-k!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F97def28d-41aa-4bb1-b74e-3ddc13b52a8e_742x682.png)

Its hoodies, tees, socks and even a basketball are understated and a little playful, released in drops that sell out, and they say: I understand tech, and I’m not a nerd about it. That is exactly the image most of the industry is reaching for. A new brand’s logo carries no such meaning yet. Printing it on an object asks the object to lend the logo meaning, and most objects can’t.

The brands that get merch right start with two questions. Why would someone want to carry this? And what does carrying it make them part of?

Answer those well and merch becomes the cheapest invitation a brand will ever send into its world. The best pieces are made the way a good designer makes anything: by editing hard, choosing materials with intent, and knowing what to leave out. They carry the brand’s taste, its humour and its sense of place, so that someone who has never bought from you can feel what it would be like to. The product is what you sell. The merch is the atmosphere around it.

Good merch does one of three jobs: it signals, it sells, or it lets people in, and great merch captures all three.

The first brand stumbled into it.

When Glossier started shipping orders in 2014, every parcel arrived in a baby-pink bubble-wrap zip pouch. It was packaging, and customers kept it anyway. They stored makeup in it, used it as a pencil case, packed it for trips. During Paris Fashion Week in 2016, Leandra Medine carried one as a clutch. Glossier responded by selling the pouches on their own, five for $20, and the pouch became as recognisable as anything Glossier actually made .

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!16ZQ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F58ebfa07-10e6-4096-9993-db335a512429_1070x627.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!16ZQ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F58ebfa07-10e6-4096-9993-db335a512429_1070x627.png)

People photographed the pouch without being asked, because it signalled membership in a beauty culture they wanted to be seen in. The pouch was Glossier’s positioning in physical form, and it was distinctive enough to need no logo at all. One colour and one material did all the work, which is what restraint looks like when it is done well.

That is what a signature buys a brand. A logo asks to be noticed. A signature object gets noticed because people want to be associated with it.

The second brand did it on purpose, and turned merch into a sales engine.

In early February 2024 Hailey Bieber posted a mirror selfie holding a pastel silicone phone case with a slot moulded to fit a Rhode lip tint. The internet spent three weeks asking whether it was real. On 27 February it went on sale for $35, sold out within minutes, and kept selling out through restocks until Rhode made it a permanent line in new colours. Benefit and Colourpop posted parody videos taping their own products to phones, which only spread Rhode’s idea further.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!v7bw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F449bffd4-c1f1-4b35-99ba-ea712a1def0a_900x627.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!v7bw!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F449bffd4-c1f1-4b35-99ba-ea712a1def0a_900x627.png)

The case solved a small, real problem: you always have your phone, and you can never find your lip balm. It was designed around how the product gets used, so every case sold created a reason to buy the tint that sits inside it, and then another tint in a new shade. A case and a tint together cost $51, and Glossy quoted one observer calling the case an excellent way to grow basket size and keep lip-tint collectors coming back. The merch sold the product, and the product gave the merch a reason to exist. Form followed function so closely that the two became one object.

This is the case that should matter most to a founder watching the budget. Merch made to live alongside your product raises the value of every order.

he third brand shows what merch can do for people who can’t yet afford the product.

Rivian makes electric trucks and SUVs that most people won’t buy this year. What it offers everyone is a way of life. The company’s stated mission is to “keep the world adventurous forever” ([University of Illinois Research Park](https://researchpark.illinois.edu/tenant_directory/rivian)), and its merch is built to get you outside. When Rivian opened its Gear Shop alongside its stock-market debut in 2021, the usual mugs, tees and hoodies sat next to a camp kitchen, a tent designed to pitch on the R1T truck and an off-road recovery kit ([InsideEVs](https://insideevs.com/news/547050/rivian-gear-shop-sustainable-adventures/)). Today the shop sells a two-burner induction travel kitchen that folds into its own carrying case, a rooftop tent made with iKamper and traction boards made with MAXTRAX. In 2023 it added an apparel line, In Case of Adventure, with New York designer Greg Jackson, built around function and utility and priced from $40 to $225

Every piece answers the question the trucks are built around: where are you going this weekend? A fleece for chopping firewood, a bottle for the trail, a stove for dinner by the lake. Together they make the brand’s belief tangible: the outdoors is worth getting to, and worth protecting. Someone who buys into that belief through a fleece or a camp stove has already stepped into Rivian’s world, years before the truck.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NK6D!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5e10448b-cbc0-4088-8b0b-59da62f272b5_1064x946.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NK6D!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5e10448b-cbc0-4088-8b0b-59da62f272b5_1064x946.png)

Rivian even has a signature character to carry. When someone walks up to a parked Rivian, a small yeti in a red vest pops up on the screen to let them know the cameras are watching. Owners nicknamed him Gary . Rivian now sells him as a plush, a pocket tee with the yeti peeking out, and limited Halloween drops in which he turns vampire . Only insiders know the joke, and that is exactly why people want it.

A hiker in a Rivian fleece isn’t buying a truck this year. She is wearing the brand on the trail, cooking on its stove at the campsite, and noticing every R1T that passes her on the highway. When she is ready, there is only one truck on her list. She may never buy it, and she will still tell her friends about it, which is its own return. The truck stays at the centre. Everything around it gives more people a reason to belong.

So what should a brand do on Monday morning, especially a young one without Rivian’s budget or Glossier’s history? Treat merch the way a designer treats a commission: with a brief, a point of view and the discipline to edit.

**Start with thinking.** Before choosing an object, decide what you want it to say, how it relates to your brand and who you want it to let in. Look at how your customers use your product, and design something that sits next to it. If your product lives outdoors, make the thing they take outdoors. If it lives on a desk, make the thing that earns its place on that desk. A useful object built around your product will sell more of the product.

**Make it signature.** Aim for an object people recognise across a room without reading anything on it, the way they recognise Glossier pink. A colour, a shape, a material, a detail only insiders catch. Leave the logo small or leave it off. Restraint is a design decision, and usually the best one on the table.

**Collaborate and co-create.** If budgets are tight, find a brand that shares your customer’s values and design something together. You split the cost, borrow each other’s credibility and reach two communities at once. Rivian built its gear with specialist outdoor brands; a small skincare label can do the same with the salon its customers already love.

**Make it scarce.** Limited drops tied to a season, a city or an event turn an object into a memory, and give people a reason to show up. When people feel lucky to own something, they photograph it and post it without being asked, because posting it says they belong. Restock what people love and retire what has run its course, so the scarcity stays real.

**Put it where people can buy it.** Too many brands make good merch and then hide it inside PR boxes. Sell it on your website and in your store. Every piece that leaves your shop is free marketing for as long as it lives, on a commute, in a photo, on a stranger’s shoulder in another city.

**Make some of it earned.** Some merch should never be for sale. Because no amount of money can buy it, it sends the strongest signal of all, and for a young brand it is also the cheapest to make. Pick a behaviour worth rewarding, like a tenth visit, a first referral or a year as a customer, and make something only those people can have. Then make sure everyone knows what it takes to get one.

**Wait if you can’t do it well yet.** Making nothing is cheaper than making landfill, and it does less damage to how people see you. Hire someone who knows how, or hold the budget until there is an idea worth spending it on. Give your customer more credit.

My alag cap has been through a monsoon, a summer in Berlin and more café queues than I can count. It has faded a little at the brim, the way good cotton does, and I like it more for it. In Berlin, the cap started conversations with strangers who had been to Goa and wanted to know if I’d been to alag too. A small café in Siolim will never know how many of those conversations it started.

That is the return every brand should want from merch: an object that keeps the relationship going long after the sale, invites new people in, and sends the existing ones back for more. The brands that understand this already treat merch as a main act, designed with as much care as the product itself. The rest are filling donation boxes.

kept.heading: HOW LONG SHOULD A REEL BE? UNDER 3 MINUTES ON INSTAGRAM, LONGER ON TIKTOK (12 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Video length barely matters on Instagram until the 3-minute mark, where recommendations to new audiences stop. Reels from 10 seconds to 3 minutes all perform within 2% of each creator's median, while longer ones fall to 0.91x. TikTok rewards length instead, with 3-to-10-minute videos earning 1.22x and beating the same creator's 10-to-19-second clips for 68% of creators.
kept.article_text:
Title: How long should a reel be? Under 3 minutes on Instagram, longer on TikTok

URL Source: https://virev.ai/blog/how-long-should-a-reel-be

Published Time: 2026-10-15

Markdown Content:
On Instagram, reels under 10 seconds earn the most views against the creator's own median, at 1.02x, but every length up to 3 minutes lands within 2% of it, so any length under 3 minutes works. Reels over 3 minutes drop to 0.91x. On TikTok, 3 to 10 minute videos earn the most, at 1.22x the creator's median.

We compared each video with its own creator's median video, so a few big accounts do not decide the answer. The sample is 10,510,431 public Instagram reels and 3,272,302 TikToks from accounts with 1,000 or more followers, posted from August 2025 to September 2026.

Most pages that rank for this question give a range such as 7 to 15 seconds, or 45 to 60 seconds, from experience or from one pooled sample. Socialinsider's 45 to 60 second answer reads the median views of all reels in each length bracket, with 4,700 for reels of 1 to 30 seconds and 10,374 for 45 to 60 seconds. Pooled medians like these favor the lengths that big accounts post, as the table further down shows. This page adds the same-creator comparison, the cut by follower count, TikTok next to Instagram, and the lengths creators post.

1.00-1.02x

Reels, 10 s to 3 min

Views against the creator's own median reel. Length inside this range barely matters.

0.91x

Reels over 3 min

Instagram does not recommend these to new audiences, and they get fewer plays.

1.22x

TikToks, 3-10 min

The best TikTok length band against the creator's own median.

## How long should a reel be on Instagram

For each reel we divided its plays by the median plays of the same creator's reels in the sample. A reel at 1.00x got a normal number of plays for that creator. We then took the median of that ratio for each length band.

![Image 1: Bar chart of median views against the creator's own median, by video length. Instagram reels: 1.02x under 10 seconds, 1.00x from 10 to 89 seconds, 1.02x at 90 seconds to 3 minutes, 0.91x at 3 to 10 minutes and 0.76x past 10 minutes. TikTok: 1.02x under 10 seconds, 0.98x at 10 to 29 seconds, 1.00x to 1.01x from 30 to 89 seconds, 1.08x at 90 seconds to 3 minutes, 1.22x at 3 to 10 minutes and 1.13x past 10 minutes.](https://virev.ai/_blog/covers/how-long-should-a-reel-be/chart-length-vs-own-median.webp)

Median of each video's views divided by its creator's median video. 10,510,431 reels and 3,272,302 TikToks.

This table splits the Instagram result by follower count. "Beats median" is the share of reels in that band that got more plays than their creator's median reel, and the last six columns are the median plays against the creator's own median.

| Length | Share | Beats median | All | Nano | Micro | Mid | Macro | Mega |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Under 10 s | 8.2% | 51.6% | 1.02x | 1.01x | 1.02x | 1.04x | 1.06x | 1.06x |
| 10-19 s | 19.7% | 49.4% | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.01x | 1.02x | 1.03x |
| 20-29 s | 14.7% | 48.4% | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x |
| 30-44 s | 16.5% | 48.6% | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 0.99x | 0.99x | 1.00x |
| 45-59 s | 12.6% | 49.0% | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 0.99x | 0.99x | 0.98x |
| 60-89 s | 14.8% | 49.2% | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 0.99x | 0.98x |
| 90 s-3 min | 11.4% | 51.2% | 1.02x | 1.02x | 1.02x | 1.02x | 1.01x | 1.01x |
| 3-10 min | 1.6% | 42.2% | 0.91x | 0.87x | 0.91x | 0.94x | 0.94x | 0.96x |
| 10 min+ | 0.3% | 31.9% | 0.76x | 0.78x | 0.78x | 0.73x | 0.66x | 0.74x |

*   Reels under 10 seconds are the best band on Instagram by a small margin, at 1.02x, and they beat their creator's median 51.6% of the time.
*   The edge for reels under 10 seconds grows with account size, from 1.01x for creators with 1,000 to 10,000 followers to 1.06x for creators with over 500,000.
*   Reels of 90 seconds to 3 minutes also reach 1.02x, so a long reel under the 3-minute line does not cost plays.
*   Reels of 3 to 10 minutes fall to 0.91x and beat their creator's median only 42.2% of the time, and reels over 10 minutes fall to 0.76x.
*   Only 1.9% of reels in the sample run past 3 minutes, so few creators pay this cost.

The drop past 3 minutes matches Instagram's own rule. The Help Center page on recording a reel says reels can run up to 20 minutes and that "reels over 3 minutes won't be recommended to new audiences". A reel past that line reaches mostly the people who already follow the account.

The gaps inside the 10 second to 3 minute range are 2% or less, so pick the length the idea needs. Our [Instagram algorithm study](https://virev.ai/blog/instagram-algorithm) found that a Collab post got 1.52 times the views of the same creator's own reels, a far bigger gap than any length under 3 minutes shows.

## Best length for a TikTok video

We ran the same comparison on TikTok. Photo posts are left out.

| Length | Share | Beats median | All | Nano | Micro | Mid | Macro | Mega |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Under 10 s | 8.9% | 50.9% | 1.02x | 1.04x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.02x |
| 10-19 s | 31.7% | 48.1% | 0.98x | 0.99x | 0.97x | 0.98x | 0.99x | 1.00x |
| 20-29 s | 14.7% | 47.8% | 0.98x | 0.98x | 0.97x | 0.97x | 0.97x | 0.97x |
| 30-44 s | 12.2% | 48.9% | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | 0.98x | 0.98x | 0.96x |
| 45-59 s | 8.6% | 49.2% | 1.00x | 1.01x | 1.00x | 0.99x | 0.97x | 0.96x |
| 60-89 s | 11.8% | 50.3% | 1.01x | 1.02x | 1.02x | 1.01x | 1.00x | 1.00x |
| 90 s-3 min | 8.9% | 53.2% | 1.08x | 1.09x | 1.11x | 1.08x | 1.07x | 1.03x |
| 3-10 min | 3.1% | 57.9% | 1.22x | 1.16x | 1.25x | 1.25x | 1.19x | 1.21x |
| 10 min+ | 0.2% | 54.6% | 1.13x | 1.27x | 1.05x | 1.12x | 1.24x | 1.09x |

*   On TikTok, videos of 90 seconds to 3 minutes get 1.08x their creator's median, and videos of 3 to 10 minutes get 1.22x.
*   The 3 to 10 minute band sits above 1.15x in every follower tier, from 1.16x for nano creators to 1.25x for micro and mid-size creators.
*   10 to 29 second videos, the most common lengths on TikTok, sit slightly below the creator's median at 0.98x.
*   Videos over 10 minutes are 0.2% of the sample, so their 1.13x rests on 5,797 videos.

TikTok's [Creator Rewards Program](https://support.tiktok.com/en/business-and-creator/creator-rewards-program/creator-rewards-program) pays only for videos that are at least one minute long, which gives creators with 10,000+ followers a reason to post longer. The gain also shows up for creators with 1,000 to 10,000 followers, who cannot join the program. Our [TikTok algorithm study](https://virev.ai/blog/tiktok-algorithm) measured length within the same creator and month with a different model and found the same order, with length the factor that moved views most.

## Same creator, short against long

The tables above compare each video with the creator's overall median. A stricter test takes creators who posted at least two videos in a band and at least two in the 10 to 19 second band, and compares the two medians for each creator. "Win" is the share of those creators whose median in the band beat their 10 to 19 second median, and "ratio" is the typical creator's band median divided by their 10 to 19 second median.

| Length | Reel creators | Reels win | Reels ratio | TikTok creators | TikToks win | TikTok ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Under 10 s | 100,276 | 55.1% | 1.06x | 28,062 | 56.7% | 1.09x |
| 20-29 s | 158,394 | 49.1% | 0.99x | 39,569 | 51.1% | 1.01x |
| 30-44 s | 150,744 | 49.0% | 0.99x | 34,421 | 53.9% | 1.06x |
| 45-59 s | 120,819 | 49.5% | 0.99x | 26,875 | 55.4% | 1.10x |
| 60-89 s | 109,002 | 49.1% | 0.99x | 23,953 | 57.9% | 1.18x |
| 90 s-3 min | 75,828 | 50.4% | 1.01x | 18,443 | 61.5% | 1.28x |
| 3-10 min | 14,735 | 41.2% | 0.84x | 7,555 | 68.2% | 1.59x |
| 10 min+ | 2,161 | 25.9% | 0.59x | 435 | 69.9% | 1.80x |

*   On Instagram, 55.1% of 100,276 creators got more plays on their under-10-second reels than on their 10 to 19 second reels, and the typical gain was 6%.
*   From 20 seconds to 3 minutes, Instagram creators split about evenly, so neither length wins for most of them.
*   Only 41.2% of Instagram creators did better with their 3 to 10 minute reels, and the typical creator got 0.84x.
*   On TikTok, the share of creators who did better rises with every step in length, from 51.1% at 20 to 29 seconds to 68.2% at 3 to 10 minutes.
*   For the 7,555 TikTok creators with both lengths, a 3 to 10 minute video got a median 1.59x the views of the same creator's 10 to 19 second videos.

## Why other studies say 45 to 60 seconds

If you pool every reel and read the median plays for each length, longer reels look far better. The pooled columns below are the median views of all videos in each band, from the same sample without the per-creator step, and the other columns repeat the per-creator result.

| Length | Reels pooled | Reels vs own | TikTok pooled | TikTok vs own |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Under 10 s | 8,383 | 1.02x | 13,000 | 1.02x |
| 10-19 s | 11,080 | 1.00x | 14,900 | 0.98x |
| 20-29 s | 11,432 | 1.00x | 14,900 | 0.98x |
| 30-44 s | 12,565 | 1.00x | 21,500 | 1.00x |
| 45-59 s | 14,337 | 1.00x | 26,700 | 1.00x |
| 60-89 s | 17,125 | 1.00x | 50,600 | 1.01x |
| 90 s-3 min | 18,315 | 1.02x | 59,600 | 1.08x |
| 3-10 min | 7,528 | 0.91x | 61,100 | 1.22x |
| 10 min+ | 3,886 | 0.76x | 32,200 | 1.13x |

*   Pooled together, reels of 90 seconds to 3 minutes get 2.2 times the median plays of reels under 10 seconds (18,315 against 8,383).
*   Against each creator's own median, both bands get 1.02x.
*   The pooled gap comes from who posts long reels, since creators with over 1 million followers post a median reel of 45 seconds and creators with 1,000 to 10,000 followers post 32 seconds.

A study that compares lengths across accounts mostly measures which accounts post which length. To decide your own length, compare your own reels with each other.

## Three creators whose results depend on length

We picked these from creators who posted many videos in both short and long bands. We checked each public profile in the browser on October 15, 2026.

| Creator | Platform | Followers at our read | Videos in sample | 10-19 s median | 3-10 min median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [@christina.the.doggroomer](https://www.tiktok.com/@christina.the.doggroomer) | TikTok | 205,303 | 97 | 40,200 (5 videos) | 143,200 (43 videos) |
| [@yaseminreads](https://www.tiktok.com/@yaseminreads) | TikTok | 35,347 | 98 | 15,000 (9 videos) | 91,150 (68 videos) |
| [@robertovalenzuela.jr](https://www.instagram.com/robertovalenzuela.jr/) | Instagram | 48,753 | 93 | 32,719 (14 reels) | 10,896 (28 reels) |

Christina, a dog groomer in the UK, posts long "day in the life" videos about her grooming work, and her profile groups 161 of them in one playlist. Her 3 to 10 minute videos got a median 143,200 views, 3.6 times her 10 to 19 second clips. Her profile showed 214.4K followers on October 15.

Yasemin posts long reading vlogs and jewelry jar videos in Turkish. 68 of her 98 videos ran 3 to 10 minutes, with a median of 91,150 views, 6.1 times her 10 to 19 second videos. She had 36.7K followers on October 15.

Roberto Valenzuela posts reels from Rancho la Alemania, a farm in Hermosillo, Sonora, his profile says. His 14 reels of 10 to 19 seconds got a median 32,719 plays, and his 28 reels of 3 to 10 minutes got 10,896, a third as many. He had 50.2K followers on October 15.

All three post long videos often, so their long medians come from many videos. The two TikTok creators gained from length, and the Instagram creator lost plays with it, which is the platform split in the tables above.

## Average Instagram reel length

The median reel in our sample is 36 seconds long and the mean is 54 seconds. The median TikTok is 25 seconds and the mean 47 seconds.

![Image 2: Line chart of the share of videos at each length from 0 to 3 minutes in 2-second steps. Both lines peak at 15 seconds, TikTok at about 11% and Instagram at about 5%. The TikTok median is 25 seconds and the reel median 36 seconds. Both lines spike at 1 minute, and the Instagram line spikes again at 90 seconds.](https://virev.ai/_blog/covers/how-long-should-a-reel-be/chart-length-distribution.webp)

Length of each video in the sample, in 2-second steps up to 3 minutes.

| Followers | Reels median | Reels mean | Reels 60 s+ | TikTok median | TikTok mean | TikTok 60 s+ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All | 36 s | 54 s | 28.2% | 25 s | 47 s | 23.9% |
| Nano, 1K-10K | 32 s | 51 s | 24.1% | 18 s | 34 s | 11.3% |
| Micro, 10K-100K | 34 s | 52 s | 26.7% | 24 s | 45 s | 21.7% |
| Mid, 100K-500K | 41 s | 58 s | 32.5% | 33 s | 55 s | 31.2% |
| Macro, 500K-1M | 44 s | 61 s | 35.6% | 37 s | 59 s | 35.2% |
| Mega, 1M+ | 45 s | 64 s | 36.9% | 39 s | 62 s | 36.1% |

*   15 seconds is the most common length on both apps, with 310,002 reels and 252,042 TikToks at exactly 15 seconds.
*   42.7% of reels and 55.3% of TikToks run under 30 seconds.
*   Both apps show a spike at 1 minute, and reels show a second spike at 90 seconds, the reel limit until January 2025.
*   Bigger accounts post longer videos, and on TikTok the median video from a creator with over 1 million followers runs 39 seconds, more than twice the 18 seconds from a creator with 1,000 to 10,000 followers.

## How long can a reel be

These are the limits each app states in its own help pages, read on October 15, 2026.

| App | Longest video | Rule that changes reach or pay |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Instagram Reels | 20 minutes, recorded or edited in Reels | Reels over 3 minutes are not recommended to new audiences. |
| TikTok | 10 minutes recorded in the app, 60 minutes uploaded | Creator Rewards pays only for videos of 1 minute or more. |

*   The [Instagram Help Center](https://help.instagram.com/2720958398006062/) says you can record and edit reels up to 20 minutes, and that reels over 3 minutes won't be recommended to new audiences.
*   Instagram raised the upload limit from 90 seconds to 3 minutes on January 17, 2025, when Adam Mosseri [posted](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DE-DISgytMe/) that the old limit was "just too short" for longer stories.
*   [TikTok's camera tools page](https://support.tiktok.com/en/using-tiktok/creating-videos/camera-tools) says videos you record in TikTok can be up to 10 minutes long, and videos you upload up to 60 minutes.

## What to do with this

### For creators

*   On Instagram, keep reels under 3 minutes, and within that range use the length the idea needs, because length moves plays by 2% or less there.
*   If you want to test short reels on Instagram, a reel under 10 seconds beat the same creator's 10 to 19 second reels for 55% of creators.
*   On TikTok, try videos of 90 seconds or longer if you have the material, since 3 to 10 minute videos beat the same creator's short clips for 68% of creators.
*   To check your own account, take your videos that are at least a week old, find your median, and see which length bands sit above it, as in our guide to [comparing reel performance at the same age](https://virev.ai/blog/compare-reel-performance-at-the-same-age).
*   For what counts as a breakout against your own median, see [how many views is viral](https://virev.ai/blog/how-many-views-is-viral).

### For brands

*   Do not ask an Instagram creator for a reel over 3 minutes if you want reach beyond their followers, because Instagram will not recommend it to new audiences.
*   On TikTok, a creator who already posts long videos well may give a product more time on screen without losing views.
*   Look at a creator's own videos at the length you plan to book, because Christina's long videos got 3.6 times the views of her short ones.
*   [Virev creator search](https://virev.ai/en/discovery?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_content=how-long-should-a-reel-be&utm_campaign=creator-discovery) covers 180M+ creators on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube and shows each one's recent videos with their views, so you can see which formats work for a creator before you book.

[Start a 3-day trial](https://virev.ai/en/sign-up?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_content=how-long-should-a-reel-be&utm_campaign=creator-discovery) to run your first search.

## How we measured, and what can be wrong

*   The Instagram sample is the reels set of our [Instagram algorithm study](https://virev.ai/blog/instagram-algorithm), which holds public creator accounts with 1,000 or more followers and removes brands, shops, media and giveaway posts.
*   From that set we kept reels with a length and at least 1 play, from creators with 5 or more such reels, which leaves 10,510,431 reels from 301,713 creators.
*   Instagram reel plays come from our read of the public play count, and the length is the video length Instagram reports.
*   The TikTok sample is the video set of our [TikTok algorithm study](https://virev.ai/blog/tiktok-algorithm), which holds public creator accounts with 1,000 or more followers and 10 or more videos and removes videos tagged as ads or giveaways.
*   From that set we dropped photo posts and kept videos with at least 1 view from creators with 5 or more videos, which leaves 3,272,302 videos from 53,160 creators.
*   Follower tiers use the follower count at our read, with nano at 1,000 to 10,000, micro at 10,000 to 100,000, mid at 100,000 to 500,000, macro at 500,000 to 1 million and mega over 1 million.
*   Views keep growing after posting, and the videos had different ages at our read.
*   When we compared each video only with the same creator's videos from the same month, the pattern held, with reels of 3 to 10 minutes at 0.95x and TikToks of 3 to 10 minutes at 1.12x.
*   When we kept only reels 7 to 89 days old at the read, reels of 3 to 10 minutes got 0.92x.
*   The sample holds only videos that were still public when we read them, so a creator who deleted weak long videos, or weak short ones, would make that length look better than it was.
*   Creators choose a length for each idea, and a creator may save a long video for a strong topic, so part of the long-video gain on TikTok may come from the topic.
*   Instagram reels in the sample include Collab posts and paid partnerships, and without them the result is the same, with 1.03x under 10 seconds, 1.01x at 90 seconds to 3 minutes and 0.89x at 3 to 10 minutes.
*   Short reels loop, so if Instagram counts a replay as another play, part of the edge for reels under 10 seconds may come from replays.
*   Our crawler collects accounts for creator marketing, so the sample holds more active creators than each app as a whole, and some news and TV pages that call themselves creators.
*   The study does not cover YouTube Shorts, because the exports it uses hold Instagram and TikTok only.

## Download the data

The tables behind every chart are in one CSV: [how-long-should-a-reel-be-2026.csv](https://virev.ai/_blog/covers/how-long-should-a-reel-be/how-long-should-a-reel-be-2026.csv). Each row has a table name, a platform, a follower tier and a length band. The tables are length_vs_own_median (videos, creators, share of videos, median views against the creator's own median, share beating the creator's median), paired_vs_10_19s, pooled_median_views and length_posted. Please cite "Virev, October 2026" and link this page.

kept.heading: YOUR NEWSLETTER ISN'T THE UNSUBSCRIBE PROBLEM (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Google Postmaster Tools evaluates unsubscribe compliance across all email systems sending from the same domain. If someone unsubscribes from a newsletter but still receives CRM or sales emails, Google may flag the domain. Sync unsubscribe lists across platforms and use distinct From addresses and List-IDs for each mailing list. Verify that every system supports one-click unsubscribes and removes recipients within 48 hours. Compliance status can take 1-2 weeks to update.
kept.article_text:
Title: Your newsletter isn't the unsubscribe problem

URL Source: https://www.audiencebridge.io/p/your-newsletter-isn-t-the-unsubscribe-problem

Published Time: 2026-10-07T19:20:42.829Z

Markdown Content:
If Postmaster Tools is showing **"Needs work"** next to Honor unsubscribe, your newsletter platform probably isn't the problem.

You checked it. The one-click header is there. Unsubscribes process instantly. Everything on the newsletter side looks clean, and the status still won't flip.

![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/83bb4a1d-af12-48bd-8bd3-143adbbfba1d/image.png?t=1791395040)

Here's the thing.

In almost every case I've looked at, the cause is a second system sending email from the same domain.

Your newsletter goes out through beehiiv. Your automations, sales outreach or onboarding go out through HubSpot.

Same domain, two lists, and neither one knows who unsubscribed from the other.

## Google Grades Your Domain, Not Your Platform

Think about what Google can actually see.

It can't log into beehiiv or HubSpot and check your suppression list.

What it sees is a Gmail user hit unsubscribe on your email, and then whether more of your email kept showing up in that inbox afterward.

That's the whole test.

Google's rule is that once someone unsubscribes, they're off the list within 48 hours. And it counts the unsubscribe whether or not your servers ever received the request.

If someone tapped the button and mail kept coming, that's on you.

Now here's the part that catches people.

Google measures this per domain.

So your newsletter, your HubSpot automations, your sales sequences and your onboarding emails all get graded together if they come from the same domain.

One sloppy system drags the whole domain to "Needs work."

## Two Systems, One Domain, Nobody Talking

Here's how it plays out.

A subscriber is on your newsletter in beehiiv.

They're also in HubSpot, because they downloaded a guide, booked a demo, or got pulled into a sales sequence. Both systems send from **your-domain(dot)com**.

They get tired of hearing from you and hit unsubscribe in Gmail on the newsletter.

beehiiv removes them right away.

Perfect.

Two days later, HubSpot sends them a nurture email from the same domain, often from the same person's name.

HubSpot has no idea they unsubscribed, because the unsubscribe never left beehiiv.

From where Gmail sits, that person told you to stop, and you didn't.

Google does let you run separate lists.

Its guidance is that each mailing list should have its own List-ID or its own From address, so an unsubscribe only takes someone off the list it came from.

But most setups I see don't separate them cleanly.

Same From address, no distinct List-ID, and the reader can't tell the difference between your newsletter and your outreach.

Neither can Gmail.

And moving HubSpot to a subdomain doesn't hide it. Subdomain data still counts toward the primary domain.

## The Next Button They Hit Is Spam

It's easy to treat "Needs work" as a compliance checkbox.

It isn't.

It's a preview of your next complaint.

Think about the person on the other end.

They unsubscribed. Your email showed up anyway.

They're not going to look for the unsubscribe link a second time.

They're going to hit spam.

That complaint doesn't land on HubSpot.

It lands on your domain, the same one your newsletter is sending from.

So the outreach sequence nobody was watching is now dragging down inbox placement for the newsletter that actually makes you money.

I've rebuilt a domain's reputation from the ground up before. It took the better part of a year.

A sync between two systems takes an afternoon.

## Find Every System Sending as You

Start Monday by listing everything that sends email from your domain.

Not just the newsletter.

Your CRM, your sales tool, your billing system, your webinar platform, your onboarding sequences.

If you're not sure, your DMARC reports will show you every source sending under your domain, including the ones nobody remembers setting up.

Then fix it in this order:

1.   **Sync unsubscribes between systems.** An unsubscribe in beehiiv should suppress that person in HubSpot, and the other way around. Use an integration or a scheduled sync, but don't rely on someone remembering to export a CSV.

2.   **Separate your mail streams.** Give your newsletter and your outreach their own From address and their own List-ID, so an unsubscribe from one is clearly scoped to that list.

3.   **Check headers everywhere.** Every system sending marketing email needs one-click unsubscribe, not just your newsletter platform.

Then give it time and watch the status.

It can take a week or two for it to flip compliant.

If it doesn't flip, there's still a system out there you haven't found.

See you next week,

Chris Miquel

_P.S. The hardest part of fixing this one is finding the second system. If your Postmaster Tools is showing "Needs work" and you can't find the cause,_ _**send me a reply**_ _._

kept.heading: A STANDING HOLDOUT IS THE ONLY AUDIT AN ALGORITHM CANNOT ARGUE WITH (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Standing holdouts are a measurement method that reserves a portion of markets or audiences from automated ad campaigns to measure whether advertising generates incremental sales. Uber cut $100 million of its $150 million annual rider acquisition budget without reducing app installs, while Airbnb recovered to 95% of its 2019 traffic levels before resuming marketing spend. A standing holdout reserves 5% to 10% of markets and rotates them on a fixed schedule to measure advertising performance over time. Each test defines its markets, measurement period, success thresholds, and budget decisions in advance. If holdout results conflict with the platform's reported returns beyond a predefined margin, the holdout results determine budget decisions.
kept.article_text:
Title: A Standing Holdout Is the Only Audit an Algorithm Cannot Argue With

URL Source: https://karandhir.substack.com/p/a-standing-holdout-is-the-only-audit

Published Time: 2026-10-14T18:01:34+00:00

Markdown Content:
In 2017, Uber’s head of performance marketing, Kevin Frisch, had a problem that had nothing to do with measurement. The company’s ads were showing up on Breitbart, the site was on Uber’s blacklist, and no ad network would admit to placing them. So Frisch started switching networks off one at a time to find the culprit. He turned off 10% of the roughly $150 million a year Uber was spending to acquire riders, and nothing happened to rider sign-ups. So he kept switching networks off, one after another. As he told the Marketing Today podcast in early 2020, Uber eventually turned off $100 million of the $150 million, two-thirds of the budget, and saw no change in the number of rider app installs. One of the networks involved, Phunware, later paid Uber $6 million to settle a fraud claim. The reporting had said the spend was working for years, and Frisch’s own conclusion from the episode was that a company needs someone who has no stake in the spend continuing, because everyone attached to the budget had a reason to believe the reporting.

That same spring, JPMorgan Chase found its ads next to fake news through a New York Times inquiry. Kristin Lemkau, the bank’s chief marketing officer, cut the number of sites running Chase display ads from about 400,000 a month to about 5,000 that a human had approved. She told the Times a few days later that the cost of impressions and the visibility of the ads had barely moved. A 99% cut in placements produced no measurable loss.

Procter & Gamble ran the largest version of the test. In the April to June quarter of 2017, P&G cut more than $100 million of digital spend after finding ads served to bots and placed on sites that did not meet its standards. On the July earnings call, CFO Jon Moeller told reporters that the company did not see a reduction in its growth rate, which told him the spending it cut had been largely ineffective. P&G cut another $100 million through December. At the ANA conference in March 2018, chief brand officer Marc Pritchard put the full-year figure at $200 million, said the company had reduced spend with several large platforms by 20% to 50%, and gave the detail that explained it: the average view time of an ad in a mobile newsfeed was 1.7 seconds.

Airbnb ran the accidental version of the same test. When the pandemic hit in 2020, the company cut marketing to almost nothing because bookings had collapsed. In 2019 it had increased performance marketing by $314 million and brand spend by $160 million. On the fourth quarter earnings call in February 2021, Brian Chesky told investors that traffic had come back to 95% of 2019 levels before any marketing spend resumed, and that in the fourth quarter more than 90% of traffic was direct or unpaid. He said Airbnb would never again spend the same share of revenue on marketing as it had in 2019, and it has not.

That is four companies in four industries, and one method between them. Each learned what its spend was doing by turning the spend off. None of them learned it from a dashboard, and none of them planned the test. Uber was chasing a brand safety problem. Chase was embarrassed by a newspaper. P&G was cleaning up a supply chain. Airbnb was simply trying to survive the year. Adidas, whose Latin American paid search went down by accident in 2017 with no effect on traffic, makes a fifth, and I covered it last week. The truth about $100 million a year at Uber had been sitting there, available to anyone willing to switch something off, and it took a scandal to run the experiment.

Last week I described how automated buying systems bid toward the conversions their own models count and then report on those counts. The reason that arrangement cannot audit itself is the same reason Facebook’s own researchers found in 2019 when they compared observational measurement to 15 randomized experiments, and again in 2023 across hundreds more: the systems target people who were already going to convert, and no adjustment on the data you can see removes a selection process running on data you cannot. An automated bidder is that selection process. It finds the people closest to a purchase, pays for their attention, and records the purchase as its own. The report will always be favorable because the machine is scored on the thing it was built to find.

A holdout breaks that circle with one move. You choose, before anything runs, a group that will get no ads: a set of markets, a set of households, a share of an audience. Afterward you compare what happened in that group to what happened everywhere else. The machine has no way to argue with the comparison, because the held-out group never entered its auction. There is no modeled conversion to dispute, no attribution window to debate, and no claim about who would have bought anyway. The counterfactual is sitting in the control group, counted by your own systems.

Most companies that run holdouts run them the way Uber did, once, under pressure, and then stop. A test answers one question about one channel in one window, and then the organization goes back to reading the dashboard. A standing holdout is a permanent line in the media plan. A share of markets is always held out of the automated campaigns, the set rotates on a schedule so no sales region carries the cost for long, the analysis plan is written and dated before each rotation, and the results land on the same calendar as the model refresh and the budget review. The accident Uber had becomes infrastructure.

The holdout should sit against the automated campaigns specifically, because those are the campaigns grading themselves. Manual campaigns can share the holdout, and the model refresh will use the read for every channel, but the question the holdout exists to answer is what the machine did with the authority it was given. In practice that means the held-out markets are excluded from Performance Max, Advantage+ and whatever automated products the other platforms are selling that quarter, with the exclusion set at the campaign level and checked in the placement reports, because a holdout the machine can leak into is a holdout in name only.

The pattern has a long record. eBay held out about 30% of US markets from brand search for 60 days in 2012 and found close to zero incremental sales. Netflix, as I wrote in September, treats the takedown of a campaign as a second experiment and the relaunch in fresh markets as a third, which turns one intervention into three reads. Booking runs its experimentation program at 25,000 tests a year and keeps every result in a searchable archive. The companies with the best measurement in the world got there by keeping a control group alive at all times, and the dashboards came second.

Here is the part that has changed in the last year. In May 2025, Google cut the minimum budget for an incrementality test in Google Ads from roughly $100,000 to $5,000, using Bayesian methods it says produce conclusive results more often, and it expanded the program again that November. Google says the new approach makes results up to 50% more conclusive, which is a claim about statistics rather than about your business, and it is still a claim worth taking, because a cheap randomized read beats an expensive modeled one on every channel where it is available. Meta has sold Conversion Lift studies for years. The platforms have decided that holdouts are a feature, and that is good news, because it means a randomized test on a single channel is now cheap enough for almost any advertiser.

Those studies belong in your portfolio, under the classification rules from last month: randomized assignment with a documented mechanism, pre-agreed statistical power, and an outcome that reconciles to your definitions. Use them wherever they fit the question you are asking. Then notice exactly what those studies measure. A platform lift study measures the platform’s channel, on the platform’s conversion definition, inside the platform’s reporting. It does not measure what the automated campaign did to your brand search, your existing customers, your other channels, or your ledger. A geo holdout you own and run against the whole automated program is the only instrument that measures the thing you actually bought. Both have a place in the portfolio, and only one of them is an audit.

I run measurement for a large marketing portfolio, and the standing holdout against automated buying is the line I would defend last if forced to cut. The design choices are well documented, and almost none of them are statistical. They are management decisions wearing statistical clothing, and they belong to whoever owns the budget.

Size is the first decision, and the hardest one. Advertising effects are small relative to the normal variance in sales, so a holdout large enough to produce a clear answer is one that the sales team will feel. Five to ten percent of markets, for long enough to see carryover, is the range where answers become usable. A holdout sized for political comfort produces a result everyone reads according to their existing position.

Rotation is the second decision, and it is the one that makes the first one bearable. The held-out markets change on a fixed schedule, quarterly in most plans, so the cost of learning moves around the organization and no regional leader can claim a permanent penalty. Rotation also produces the repetition that turns one read into stable knowledge.

Protection is the governance object, and it needs an owner. National promotions, launches and platform changes get scheduled around the holdout window or the window moves, and a named executive owns that calendar. A company that cannot protect a test window cannot run a holdout, however good its statisticians are.

Pre-registration is the integrity object, and it is the cheapest of the five. The markets, the outcome, the analysis window and the decision thresholds are written down with a date before the rotation begins. A holdout analyzed after the results are visible is a retrofit, and a retrofit finds what its author needs.

Thresholds are the decision object, and they are the step most programs skip. Every rotation names, in advance, what result changes what budget. If the automated campaign’s reported return and the holdout’s measured return disagree by more than a stated margin, the holdout wins and the budget moves. Without that rule written down, the dashboard wins every argument, because it reports more often and reports better news.

The objection I hear most is that the company cannot afford to go dark anywhere, because every held-out market is lost revenue. The four companies at the top of this piece are the answer. Uber turned off two-thirds of its budget and lost nothing, which means the cost of not holding out had been $100 million a year. Chase cut 99% of its placements and lost nothing measurable. P&G cut $200 million and did not see its growth rate move. Airbnb went to zero and kept 95% of its traffic. The cost of a holdout is visible, small, and budgeted. The cost of an unaudited machine is invisible, large, and permanent, and it is invisible precisely because nobody holds anything out.

Budget the holdout the way you budget insurance. If holding out 5% of markets costs you 5% of the modeled conversions the machine would have reported, that premium buys you the only independent read you will ever get of the other 95%. The $100 million a year Uber was wasting would have funded a standing holdout for decades. No CFO objects to that trade once it is framed as a premium. Most never see it framed at all, because the holdout competes for budget against a dashboard that promises certainty for free.

A standing holdout tells you what the automated campaign actually did. It does not tell the machine what it is allowed to do. That is a separate document, and almost nobody writes it before the budget is live. Next week is about mandates: the limits, decision rights and kill criteria that should exist before a system gets authority over spend, and what Knight Capital and Zillow paid for writing them afterward.

kept.heading: AI AGENTS BUY THROUGH YOUR OWN CHECKOUT, AND DISPUTES STILL LAND ON YOU (8 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: In-chat AI checkouts are built for physical goods sold to US buyers through big platforms. Google, Microsoft, and ChatGPT all exclude subscriptions or say nothing about them. Independent sellers instead meet agents like Amazon's Buy for Me and Meta's Muse on their own checkout pages, where guest purchase and saved-wallet support decide whether an order completes. Visa bars merchants from requiring dispute waivers on agent purchases, so chargebacks still land on the seller.
kept.article_text:
Title: AI agents buy through your own checkout, and disputes still land on you

URL Source: https://okaneland.com/study/can-an-ai-agent-buy-from-you/

Published Time: 2026-10-14T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
[Okane Land](https://okaneland.com/)[The Study](https://okaneland.com/study/)
The Study · Explainer

[Akira Sumi](https://okaneland.com/about/) · Oct 14, 2026 · 10 min read · researched

![Image 1: A hand-inked scene of two doors. On the left, an AI assistant's checkout door behind a velvet rope with a small sign reading US buyers, captioned via platforms, US buyers, subscriptions mostly excluded. On the right, a small seller's own shop door stands open and a little robot shopper walks toward it holding a payment card, captioned already open, to any agent that can finish it. Along the bottom: for a seller on their own site, the agents that can buy today mostly use that site's checkout.](https://okaneland.com/features/study/agent-checkout/hero.png)

In March, OpenAI stepped back from the checkout it had built into ChatGPT six months earlier. Its announcement said the first version [**“did not offer the level of flexibility that we aspire to provide,”**](https://openai.com/index/powering-product-discovery-in-chatgpt/) and ChatGPT now sends shoppers to finish on the merchant’s own site.

For a one-person seller on their own site, the agents that can buy from you today mostly do it the way a person does: on your own checkout page, through your own payment provider, with the usual card disputes still landing on you.

We read the merchant pages and terms of the main assistants that buy, the protocols underneath and the card networks’ rules, and checked what a small seller can switch on now.

## The short version

*   **OpenAI’s in-chat checkout is shrinking; Google’s and Microsoft’s are growing.** OpenAI’s merchant page says it is [**“moving away from a standalone Instant Checkout experience.”**](https://chatgpt.com/merchants) Google’s and Microsoft’s in-chat checkouts sell to US buyers and reach small sellers mainly through Shopify, Etsy, PayPal or Stripe.
*   **The in-chat checkouts we checked exclude subscriptions or say nothing about them.** ChatGPT’s plugin rules allow commerce [**“only for physical goods,”**](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/plugin-guidelines) Google’s checkout and Shopify’s Copilot checkout leave subscriptions out, and digital downloads appear mainly through marketplaces such as Etsy.
*   **If you sell from your own site, the agents mostly come to your checkout.** Amazon’s Buy for Me, Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s dots and Gemini’s Task agent buy on merchants’ own sites. Muse pays instantly at the more than 1 million businesses that accept Stripe’s Link.
*   **Disputes still land on you.** Visa’s rules make the cardholder answerable for an agent’s actions and forbid merchants to require buyers to waive dispute rights. No network has shifted liability for agent purchases, and Stripe’s seller terms leave disputes, refunds and transaction fraud with the seller.
*   **AI still sends little traffic.** In a Frankfurt School study of 973 online shops from August 2024 to July 2025, chatbots referred under 0.2% of visits. Ten Shopify stores tracked by an agency took 0.12% of their revenue from AI assistants this year.
*   **Buyers hesitate.** In a YouGov poll, 14% of Americans trusted AI to place orders for them. In an NMI survey, 70% said they must be able to review or override a purchase first.
*   **The useful work is on your own site.** A checkout an agent can finish, product pages with plain prices, search crawlers let in and dispute evidence kept. Use your platform’s in-chat channel when it covers what you sell.

Everything below is the evidence, read on October 14 from the programs’ own pages, the protocols and the card networks’ rulebooks.

## Three ways an agent can pay you

“An AI agent buys from you” covers three different things, and the one open to every seller is the one that runs on your own site.

![Image 2: A diagram of three ways an AI agent can pay a seller. In-chat checkout: a shopper in an AI assistant pays through the assistant's checkout, which calls the seller's checkout endpoints over a protocol such as ACP or UCP; it reaches sellers through Shopify, Etsy, PayPal or Stripe, or by application, for US buyers. Agent on your site: the shopper's agent opens the seller's own product page and checkout like a browser and pays through the seller's own payment provider; it works on any site an agent can finish. Machine payments: a software agent pays per request for the seller's API through Stripe's Machine Payments Protocol or x402. A bracket marks the seller as the one who handles card disputes on the first two paths.](https://okaneland.com/features/study/agent-checkout/three-paths.svg)

In the first, the assistant runs the checkout and calls your systems through a protocol: the Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP, from OpenAI and Stripe) or the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP, from Google and Shopify). In the second, the shopper’s agent opens your site and fills in your checkout the way a browser would. In the third, a software agent pays per request for an API, through the Machine Payments Protocol (from Stripe and Tempo) or the x402 standard. A seller of downloads, courses or subscriptions on their own site mostly lives in the second.

## The in-chat checkouts, and who they take

| Program | Status in October 2026 | Who can sell | Fee stated | Subscriptions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ChatGPT, Agentic Commerce Protocol | in-chat checkout scaled back; product discovery live in the US | Shopify and Etsy catalogs; others apply and wait | none on purchases that start in ChatGPT | not through plugins |
| Google AI Mode and Gemini, Universal Commerce Protocol | live in the US | Merchant Center sellers Google approves, or sellers connected through a platform such as Shopify | none stated | excluded |
| Microsoft Copilot Checkout | rolling out since January 8, 2026, a pilot for some merchants | English-language merchants selling to US buyers, through PayPal, Shopify or Stripe | no commission or affiliate fee | not in Shopify’s Copilot checkout; no rule found for other routes |
| Perplexity Instant Buy | live in the US with PayPal | merchants on BigCommerce, Shopware and Wix, among others | none found | no rule found |

The platforms are the front door. Shopify switches eligible stores into the AI channels by default, including direct checkout in Copilot, and its Agentic plan lets brands that do not run on Shopify list products in the same channels. At Copilot Checkout’s January launch, Stripe said US users would be able to buy from Etsy businesses in the chat. Stripe said at the launch of its Agentic Commerce Suite that platforms including Squarespace, Wix, WooCommerce and BigCommerce would use it, and a seller on Stripe directly can upload a catalog and request a connection to each agent, which the agent has to accept. Each Shared Payment Token, the credential an agent passes to the seller, costs 15 cents to issue, and Stripe’s pricing page does not say who pays it.

A custom site has no shortcut. The Agentic Commerce Protocol’s own site says implementing it lists your products nowhere, because [**“each AI platform will manage their own process”**](https://www.agenticcommerce.dev/) for who participates. OpenAI takes direct feeds by application and waitlist, and Google’s checkout runs on its approval. Google says its protocol already enables direct checkout for hundreds of thousands of brands and retailers, and in early 2026 Shopify told Forrester about 30 merchants were live with native ChatGPT checkout, against The Information’s count of a dozen.

## The agents that use your checkout

The agents a seller on their own site can meet today mostly buy on that site.

*   **Amazon Buy for Me** completes purchases on the merchant’s website, and Amazon may list a merchant’s products using public information from its site. Amazon’s FAQ says merchants do not currently pay and Amazon takes no referral fee; sellers opt in with a feed or opt out by email.
*   **Meta’s Muse**, launched in September, pays instantly wherever the seller takes Stripe’s Link, using the shopper’s saved payment method; elsewhere it uses a single-use virtual card or signs in with the shopper’s saved card. On Shopify stores it can also check out inside Muse.
*   **OpenAI’s dots**, which began rolling out at the end of September for Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise users, can buy with a card the user saved on a merchant’s website, with the user’s approval.
*   **Gemini’s Task agent** and **Chrome’s auto browse** shop on a broad range of sites, and may ask the user to take control to enter payment details. Chrome’s version is US-only and needs a paid AI Pro or Ultra plan.

None of these needs a protocol from you. What decides whether they finish is your checkout: whether it allows a guest purchase, whether it offers a saved wallet the agents use, such as Link or Google Pay, and whether a bot wall stops a signed agent before it reaches the payment form.

## The protocols underneath

The protocols behind the buttons are young and still converging. ACP is open source and still in beta. UCP’s governing council is Google and Shopify, joined by Stripe in April. Google’s Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), announced in September 2025, reached version 0.2 in April and moved to the FIDO Alliance; we found no live Google product using it.

The card networks work a layer lower, with signed HTTP requests that let a merchant’s network provider recognize an agent. Mastercard’s Agent Pay builds on Web Bot Auth, and Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol is aligned with it. Visa’s specification says merchants are not required to adopt it, and Mastercard tells merchants to switch it on at their content delivery network with no code changes. Cloudflare has counted signed agents as verified bots since July 1, with one warning for agents that act for many people: [**“you may trust the intermediary operator, but not necessarily every end user driving it.”**](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/concepts/bot/verified-bots/) For a small seller, the practical job is to check that the bot settings of your host or network provider let verified agents through.

## Who pays when the agent gets it wrong

No card network has moved the risk of agent purchases onto the agent. Visa’s rulebook (the April 2026 edition, with agent rules added in October 2025) treats the registered provider of an agent payment as the cardholder for that transaction, and makes the cardholder responsible for the agent’s actions as if they had made the purchase themselves. It forbids a merchant to require a cardholder to waive the right to dispute, agent purchases included, and its dispute chapter has no separate condition for agents. The one agent change there helps sellers a little: from October 24, 2026, an agent provider’s login ID can be one of the matching details a seller shows to contest a fraud dispute under Visa’s Compelling Evidence 3.0 rules, alongside device or IP data from earlier undisputed orders.

Mastercard’s merchant guide says standard fraud detection, chargeback rights and dispute processes apply to agent purchases. Under existing rules, fraud on a properly authenticated, tokenized payment generally falls on the card issuer; what stays with a small seller is fraud on unauthenticated payments and every dispute short of fraud. Stripe’s seller terms make the seller the merchant of record, responsible for disputes and refunds and for managing transaction fraud. Worldpay puts the state of play in one line: [**“No liability shift exists yet.”**](https://www.worldpay.com/en/insights/articles/agentic-commerce-liability-is-still-being-written)

What the network rules have not settled is the purchase that was authorized but wrong, when the agent bought what the shopper did not mean. Two companies have started on it from the other side. Stripe’s terms for agent operators make them answerable to Stripe for purchases caused by bugs, hallucinations or misinterpretations, and American Express has announced a future protection for its cardholders when a purchase strays from the intent they approved. Neither changes what a seller faces when the chargeback arrives.

## How much buying happens this way

The traffic is growing from a small base. Adobe, which measures more than a trillion visits to US retail sites, reports steep growth in visits sent by AI assistants and says those visitors converted at a 60% higher rate than other traffic in July 2026, after converting worse a year earlier; it does not publish their share of all traffic. Researchers at Frankfurt School, looking at 973 online shops, found chatbot referrals under 0.2% of traffic between August 2024 and July 2025, before most of these programs launched. Ethercycle, a Shopify agency, counted 0.10% of sessions and 0.12% of revenue from AI assistants across ten established Shopify stores from January to August 2026, $131,000 out of $109.6 million, and found direct handoffs from an agent to checkout effectively at zero. These are referral figures; nobody publishes how many purchases agents complete.

Shoppers are cautious about letting agents pay. In YouGov’s poll, about 65% of Americans said they trusted AI to compare prices and far fewer would let it put an order through. In NMI’s August survey of 1,000 US adults, 11% had used AI to complete a transaction, and seven in ten wanted the final say before any purchase went through. The forecasts run far ahead of the measurements: Morgan Stanley puts agent-driven shopping at $190 billion to $385 billion in the US by 2030, and McKinsey at up to $1 trillion of US consumer sales orchestrated by agents.

## Digital products and subscriptions

The live programs were built for physical retail. OpenAI’s plugin rules bar selling subscriptions, digital content, tokens or credits through ChatGPT plugins. Google leaves subscriptions, services such as online classes, virtual items and goods that need software installed first out of its checkout; its shopping listings allow software subscriptions only when they are prepaid and renew annually. Shopify’s help pages exclude subscriptions from the direct checkouts in Copilot and in Google AI Mode and Gemini, and its agent catalog leaves out subscription services.

The protocols themselves are wider. ACP describes support for digital goods and subscriptions, OpenAI’s product feed has a flag for digital items, and Stripe’s agentic tools accept sellers of digital content and APIs. Etsy is the clearest documented case of digital items sold this way: its help center explains how to download a digital item bought through Gemini, Google AI Mode or Copilot, and still lists ChatGPT. We found no documented case of an AI agent buying a software subscription for a user.
