Title: The usual signs that AI is working can mislead

URL Source: https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/VzgkdF

Published Time: 2026-10-13T22:35:55.961Z

Markdown Content:
**Who this is for:** you use AI at work, pay for it, or have been asked to make it pay off, and at some point someone will ask you whether it's working. By the end you'll know why the usual answers can't be trusted, and you'll have a six-step plan for finding out properly in one process.

**Skip it if** you use a chat assistant on your own work and want tips for it. This is about a process other people depend on.

**On the length:** it's a long read. The story and the six signals are in the first half. The tests that work and the plan to copy come after, then where the method stops working.

* * *

Staff swear AI saves them time. In a 2025 trial, experienced software developers said the same: afterwards they believed AI had sped them up by 20%. The clock said their tasks took 19% longer. METR, the research group that ran it, now calls that study out of date, and its 2026 follow-up with newer tools was inconclusive. But the main point still holds: people's sense of how much time AI saves them isn't reliable.

What staff say is one of six ways organisations judge whether their AI is working, and each of them can mislead you. What executives see. The person checking the AI's work. The famous failure rates. The vendors' case studies. And the audits, which at the US tax authority and the Australian Taxation Office found no regular monitoring once the AI was live.

![Image 1: Six ways organisations judge whether AI is working, each with the evidence that it can mislead: what staff say, what executives see, the person checking the AI, the famous failure rates, vendors' case studies, and the audits.](https://pub-4f2aa5e351b44f67ba6dd0bc32fe1bb2.r2.dev/blog/deploying-ai-7b.png)

_Each row is one signal, with the study that shows how it misleads._

The AI firms have noticed where things stall. In May 2026 OpenAI launched a company to put its models to work inside other firms, with "more than $4 billion of initial investment", and Anthropic announced a services venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and Goldman Sachs. OpenAI's chief operating officer, Brad Lightcap, was quoted giving the reason: customers "need help going from pilot to production". Anthropic now advertises a Technical Deployment Lead who owns "value measurement and ROI" and doesn't write production code, at a base salary of $275,000 to $380,000. The bottleneck isn't the AI. It's knowing whether it works.

The test already exists. It wasn't invented for AI. Hospitals test advice against a comparison group. Airports plant fake threats to measure their screeners. Banks covered by the UK's model risk rules are expected to test their models against rival models, and to run new and old side by side, before trusting them. Most of what the evidence says about making AI pay comes from those three places.

I put this together by running the question through the research process I use for everything. It pulls the primary sources, grades each claim by how good its evidence is, and keeps the authors' own caveats with the claim. This article takes one part of that research further. The whole of it, from who should do the implementing to what it does to people, is in my research paper: [How to implement AI in your organisation and check it's working](https://jamiewatters.work/journey/implementing-ai-in-organisations).

* * *

## Six signals, and how each one misleads

### What staff say

The developers above are the cleanest case: 16 of them, in a randomised trial, believing the opposite of what the clock showed. That matters, because self-report is the easiest number to collect. The UK government's cross-department Copilot experiment, written up in June 2025, reported 26 minutes saved a day. That number is what users said, with no comparison group. When the Department for Business and Trade evaluated the same tool in August 2025, it "did not find evidence that time savings have led to improved productivity".

### What executives see

A 2026 survey asked nearly 6,000 executives in the US, the UK, Germany and Australia what AI had done for them. Nine in ten saw no effect on their productivity or employment over the previous three years (Yotzov, Bloom and colleagues, a working paper for the US National Bureau of Economic Research).

The harder data says the same. Danish researchers linked 25,000 workers in exposed jobs to national pay records and ruled out any effect on earnings above 2% (Humlum and Vestergaard, revised March 2026). In a trial across 7,137 workers, Microsoft's own researchers found that workers offered Copilot spent 1.4 fewer hours a week on email, about two for those who actually used it, with no detectable change in the mix of work they did (Dillon and colleagues). Output per worker did rise in several of the trials below. But pay hasn't followed in the Danish records, and nine in ten executives see no effect on productivity yet. Whether redesigning the work closes that gap hasn't been tested.

### The person checking the AI

"Keep a human in the loop" is the standard reassurance, and it's the weakest of the six. In one study, 27 radiologists read mammograms with an AI's suggestion on screen (Dratsch and colleagues, 2023). When the AI was right, the very experienced readers were right 82.3% of the time. When it was wrong, they were right 45.5% of the time. The AI was simulated, there was no group reading without it, and only five of the readers were very experienced. Those three caveats are usually dropped when the study is quoted.

![Image 2: Table of mammogram reading accuracy when a simulated AI suggestion was right versus wrong. Inexperienced: 79.7% and 19.8%. Moderately experienced: 81.3% and 24.8%. Very experienced: 82.3% and 45.5%. Dratsch et al., Radiology, 2023.](https://pub-4f2aa5e351b44f67ba6dd0bc32fe1bb2.r2.dev/blog/deploying-ai-4.png)

_Accuracy held when the AI was right and fell when it was wrong, at every level of experience._

Rarity makes it worse. In another study, six radiologists looked for cancers planted in scans (Evans, Birdwell and Wolfe, 2013). When cancers were as rare as in normal screening, they missed 30%. When the same cancers were common, they missed 12%. If an AI is right nearly all the time, its mistakes are rare, and rare mistakes are the ones people miss.

Training doesn't fix it. A review of the research on people working with automated aids concluded that automation bias "cannot be prevented by training or instructions" (Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010). And a study of 41 government policies requiring human oversight of algorithms found that people "defer to automated systems", and that the requirements "provide a false sense of security" (Green, 2022).

### The famous failure rates

You'll hear "70% of change programmes fail" in nearly every pitch. It started as a reengineering estimate in Hammer and Champy's 1993 book, reported in secondary sources as their "unscientific estimate". Hammer was later quoted saying it had been "transmogrified and distorted into a normative statement". A review of the sources found "no valid and reliable empirical evidence" for the 70% (Hughes, 2011).

"95% of AI pilots fail" comes from an MIT report whose own limitations section concedes that its six-month window "may be insufficient". My [paper on why AI projects fail](https://jamiewatters.work/journey/why-ai-projects-fail) goes through that one, and the rest of the failure rates, in detail.

### The vendors' case studies

"Klarna's AI does the work of 700 agents" was a company press claim. It isn't in Klarna's filing to list its shares, and its chief executive was later reported saying service quality fell, and that it was hiring people again. "Forward deployed engineer job postings are up 800%" traces to a Financial Times report citing a job-listings site, and my research could open neither the report nor the data. Treat a vendor's figure as a claim until someone independent has checked it.

### The audits

Where government auditors have looked at AI in use, regular monitoring was missing. In May 2025 the US tax authority's inspector general reported on the AI the IRS uses to pick returns to audit. The IRS had evaluated it only before it went live. The auditors found it "has not established processes to evaluate whether the performance of AI models is better than prior methods". Australia's National Audit Office found that 74% of the Australian Taxation Office's 43 models in production had no completed data-ethics assessment, and "no evidence of structured and regular monitoring" of those models once they were live.

Where someone did measure against a comparison, some gains were real and modest, alongside tools that did nothing measurable. A customer-support assistant at a US software firm raised resolutions an hour by 15% on average (Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2025). The least experienced gained most. The most skilled gained a little speed and lost a little quality. At UCLA Health, in a trial with 238 doctors, the best AI note-taker saved about 41 seconds a note against about 18 seconds in the comparison group, according to UCLA's release on the study. On one online retail platform, seven AI uses were tested at random and four raised sales, by up to 16.3% (Fang and colleagues, a preprint; one author worked for the platform and two consulted for it). The other three uses did nothing measurable.

![Image 3: Two panels. Measured against a comparison: customer support plus 15 per cent, AI note-takers saving about 41 seconds a note against 18 in the comparison group, an online retailer where 4 of 7 AI uses raised sales by up to 16.3 per cent. Checked by auditors: the IRS, with no process to show the AI beat the old method, and the Australian Taxation Office, with no structured, regular monitoring and 74 per cent of 43 models lacking a data-ethics assessment.](https://pub-4f2aa5e351b44f67ba6dd0bc32fe1bb2.r2.dev/blog/deploying-ai-5b.png)

_The deployments that showed gains had been measured against a comparison. The two audits found no regular monitoring once the AI was live._

That isn't proof that measuring causes success: firms that measure may be different in other ways. But my earlier failure paper found the same thing. Its two success stories had both set a measurable target in advance, one that could have shown the project failing.

* * *

## The tests that already exist

None of this needs a new idea. Three fields already test the thing the audits found skipped: whether a change works, and whether the people checking it are still catching mistakes.

### Hospitals: test it against a comparison

Medicine tests software that gives clinicians advice in controlled trials. A review of 70 of them found it worked in 75% of trials when it arrived automatically in the clinician's workflow, and in none of the few where they had to go and look for it (Kawamoto and colleagues, 2005). A larger review of 162 trials didn't confirm that: advice arriving automatically made no significant difference there (Roshanov and colleagues, 2013). The two also disagree on building advice into the patient record, which helped in the first review and was linked to worse results in the second. What the larger review did find was that requiring a reason to override the advice was strongly associated with it working. Both reviews are observational, so these are associations, not proof.

So putting the AI's answer where the decision is made is a sensible design choice, not a settled finding. What the hospital evidence does show is how much you learn from comparing one group with another: without those trials, nobody would know the two reviews disagree.

### Airports: plant the threat, and measure the screener

Airports already test the people doing the checking. EU aviation security rules have required screening systems to project fictional threat images into the bags being screened. Each screener's results are stored for at least 12 months, and the screener is told when they miss one. A 2025 study of nearly 1.2 million projected images and 728 screeners found these scores predicted how screeners did in covert tests, where real prohibited items were smuggled through (Buser and colleagues, Transportation Research Part A). That shows the scores are a valid measure, on one condition: it took about 100 sufficiently hard test images per screener before an individual's score was reliable. Whether planting images keeps screeners alert is a separate claim, and nothing I found tests it.

You can do the same with anyone checking an AI's work: slip in known mistakes at a set rate and count how many each person catches. Three other things help, on weaker evidence. The first is making people record why they overrode the AI, from the hospital trials above. Pilots who felt accountable for the outcome checked more and made fewer errors (Mosier, Skitka and colleagues, 1996, a correlation). And showing information rather than a bare recommendation, according to a review of 74 clinical studies (Goddard and colleagues, 2012).

Volume works against all of it. At one firm, after AI coding tools arrived, the number of code changes submitted rose 3.1 times, while the number of reviewers rose 1.5 times (He and colleagues, a July 2026 preprint). The share of changes getting a substantive human review fell from 39% to 21%. If the number of reviewers doesn't grow with the work, a smaller share of it gets properly checked, and nobody decided that it should.

### Banks: test against a rival model, and run old and new side by side

The Prudential Regulation Authority's [model risk rules for banks](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2023/may/model-risk-management-principles-for-banks-ss) (supervisory statement SS1/23) apply to banks approved to use their own models to set capital, and cover AI used in those models. Other banks aren't bound by them. They expect banks to compare each model's answers with those of a "challenger", a separate model built to check it: in the rules' words, "comparisons of the model output with the output of available challenger models". They also expect "parallel outcomes analysis", which means running old and new side by side and comparing results, and ongoing monitoring of vendor model performance. They require a named senior manager to own model risk. An April 2026 update was a clarification, not a change of policy. In the US, the Federal Reserve's 2011 guidance (SR 11-7) asked for "effective challenge": critical analysis "by objective, informed parties". Its April 2026 replacement says generative and agentic AI models "are not within the scope of this guidance", so on generative AI the UK expectations are now the more explicit.

![Image 4: Five rows mapping bank model-risk rules to AI deployment steps: challenger comparisons to testing against a rival, parallel outcomes analysis to running new beside old, ongoing monitoring to measuring after go-live, an accountable senior manager to a named owner, effective challenge to an independent check on the AI.](https://pub-4f2aa5e351b44f67ba6dd0bc32fe1bb2.r2.dev/blog/deploying-ai-6d.png)

_UK banks with approved internal models are expected to run these checks, AI included. The current US guidance leaves generative AI out._

I've sat on the approving side. From 2023 I was a member of a bank's committee that approved AI and cloud initiatives for development and deployment. Each discipline signed off its own area: information security, infrastructure, risk, legal, compliance and finance. Most of what came to it was about data in the cloud, hosting, resilience and data moving offshore. I didn't design that process. I was a member of it.

The AI firms' job adverts show what's missing. Anthropic's forward deployed engineers build "production applications with Claude models" inside customer systems. Its separate Technical Deployment Lead owns "value measurement and ROI". None of the engineering adverts in my research mentions a challenge function: the people whose job is to try to prove the model wrong.  US bank guidance asked for it from 2011 until April 2026, when its replacement left AI out. Whether buyers outside banking will pay for it is a question the research can't answer.

* * *

## Six steps for one process

Put the three fields together and you get a method. It works on one process at a time, where you can count the result. It isn't evidence for rolling AI out across a whole company at once: my research found no randomised study of that.

![Image 5: Six steps in order: pick one process, measure today, decide each step, answer at the moment of decision, test against the old way, keep measuring, each with the evidence behind it. The four checks are highlighted.](https://pub-4f2aa5e351b44f67ba6dd0bc32fe1bb2.r2.dev/blog/deploying-ai-3c.png)

_Steps 1, 2, 5 and 6 are the checks around the AI. That is where most of the evidence is._

**1. Pick one process, one owner and one number.** Choose a single process and the person responsible for it. Then choose one result you can count, such as the cost of handling an invoice or the days it takes to settle a complaint. Then, before you build anything, write down what would make you stop. For example: "If the new process makes more mistakes than the old one, we switch it off." Research on IT projects that ran out of control backs this up (Keil and Robey, 1999). Clear criteria for success and failure helped people stop the projects that were failing.

**2. Measure how the process runs today.** Before you change anything, record how long each case takes, how often work has to be corrected or sent back, and what each case costs. This is what you'll compare the AI against later. Without it, you can't tell whether anything improved. Start with the numbers your systems already hold. Then talk to the people doing the work and watch them, because they do things the systems don't record. Give this stage a deadline. The UK government's [service manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-discovery-phase-works) says this kind of investigation typically takes "around 4 to 8 weeks". That's guidance: my research found no study of how long it should take.

**3. Decide who or what does each step.** Go through the process one step at a time, and ask these questions in order. Can we cut it? Can we simplify it? Can it become a fixed rule (if this, then that)? Can AI do it? Or must a person do it? A review of 63 studies found that fixed rules suit work that's high in volume and standardised, with few exceptions, and already digital (Wewerka and Reichert, 2020). AI only helps on tasks it's good at. In a trial with 758 consultants, AI made work better and faster on tasks it was good at, and made answers less accurate on tasks it wasn't (Dell'Acqua and colleagues, 2026). Keep a person on any step where a mistake is expensive or can't be undone, or where the law requires one. That last rule is common sense rather than research: I found no study that tests it.

**4. Put the AI's answer in front of people at the moment they decide.** Don't make anyone go and look for it in another screen or tool. That's a sensible design choice that some of the hospital evidence supports and some doesn't. When someone disagrees with the AI, make them record why: in the larger hospital review, that was strongly linked to the advice working. And review a sample of the cases where they agreed, so agreeing isn't simply the easy path.

**5. Test it against the old way, and test the people checking it.** This step has two parts.

First, run the AI version alongside the old process for a while, on the same kind of work, and compare the two using the numbers from step 2. If the AI version does better, extend it to more of the work, a piece at a time, checking the numbers each time. This is what banks are expected to do with their models.

Second, test the people who check the AI's work. Slip known mistakes into what they review, on purpose, and count how many each person catches. Do it in a copy of the work, never in live customer cases, and agree it with staff first. You need enough planted mistakes to judge a person, not a handful. If they start catching fewer, stop and fix it before you carry on. This is what airports do with fake threat images. My research paper sets out the full routine and a worksheet.

**6. Keep measuring after it goes live.** This is the step the audits found missing. Keep tracking the same numbers for as long as the AI is in use. Name the person who can switch it off, and what evidence would make them do it.

Don't expect the payoff quickly. Across firms, the measured return to AI has fallen before it rose. In US Census manufacturing data, firms' productivity dipped after they adopted AI before it improved, though the authors don't say how long the dip lasts (McElheran and colleagues, 2025). In a Deloitte survey across Europe and the Middle East, with 1,854 responses, a typical AI use case took two to four years to earn a satisfactory return, by the respondents' own account. So at three and six months, look at two things only: is it heading the right way, and is it causing any harm? Don't decide whether it paid off on one quarter's figures.

Here it is as a plan you can copy for one process.

```
SIX STEPS FOR ONE PROCESS

1  PICK ONE PROCESS      One process, one owner, one number you
                         can count. Write down what result would
                         make you stop.

2  MEASURE TODAY         Before changing anything: time per case,
                         how often work is corrected or sent back,
                         cost per case. Systems first, then the
                         people doing the work. Set a deadline.

3  DECIDE EACH STEP      For every step, ask in this order:
                         cut it? simplify it? a fixed rule?
                         AI? a person?
                         A person keeps anything costly or
                         hard to undo.

4  ANSWER AT THE         The AI's answer appears while people
   MOMENT OF DECISION    decide, without them looking for it.
                         Anyone who overrides it records why.

5  TEST AGAINST THE      Run old and new side by side. Compare
   OLD WAY               them on the step 2 numbers. Extend
                         only if the new one does better.
   TEST THE CHECKERS     In a copy of the work, never live.
                         Slip known mistakes in. Count how many
                         each reviewer catches. Fewer caught
                         means stop. Count checking time as
                         a cost.

6  KEEP MEASURING        Same numbers, after go-live. At 3 and 6
                         months: right direction? any harm?
                         Judge the payoff later, not on one
                         quarter. Name who can switch it off.
```

* * *

## Where this breaks

The method is put together from other fields. Steps four to six come from clinical decision support, airport screening and bank model risk, not from trials of AI deployment, because almost none exist. Applying them to AI is reasonable, but it's a judgement, not a tested result.

It doesn't fit company-wide bets on a single AI platform, where there's no one process to measure. It struggles with low-volume work that's mostly judgement, where there's nothing to count. And it may not hold for AI agents acting across many systems at speed, where having a person approve every action may not be possible.

[Amazon](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/AMZN/) on Thursday [unveiled](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/amazon-personal-ai-bee-frontier-bee-eclipse) two new Bee listening devices, including a wearable and a credit card-sized voice recorder, marking its latest push into the AI gadget market.

The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon’s existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing. Similar to earlier generations, the Bee Frontier has up to seven days of battery life, but it’s also more expensive, costing $75 compared with its $50 predecessor.

Amazon acquired [Bee](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/07/22/amazon-ai-bee-wearable.html), a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations.

The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, “so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn’t, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office,” Amazon said in a blog post.

Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone.

The Bee Frontier is available Thursday, while the Bee Eclipse “will be available soon,” the company said.

Amazon is refreshing its Bee lineup as tech companies gear up for the holiday season with a slew of new [AI hardware](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/14/tech-giants-race-to-get-ai-gadgets-on-shelves-for-holiday-rush.html). Amazon nixed its budget-friendly Fire family of tablets in favor of three new AI-infused [Alexa Tablets](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/08/amazon-alexa-tablet-release.html), while [Microsoft](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/MSFT/) showcased an [Nvidia](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/NVDA/)-powered Windows laptop and [Apple](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/AAPL/) unveiled its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI.

The Bee gadgets will compete with other AI wearables already on the market.

The $100 Bee Eclipse is a credit card-sized device that magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone.

[Meta](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/META/) has seen growing momentum from its smart glasses that are infused with AI and have a built-in camera. The glasses have also generated widespread privacy and civil rights concerns from users, advocacy groups and lawmakers.

Meta has also announced a palm-sized pendant called [Muse Charm](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/23/mark-zuckerberg-1299-meta-vr-glasses-ai-agent.html) that runs its latest Muse AI assistant. [Plaud](https://www.plaud.ai/pages/plaud-note-pro) developed a card-shaped note-taking device, and [Friend](https://friend.com/?page=shop) offers an AI necklace.

Amazon’s voice-activated Echo smart speaker got users comfortable with interacting with its Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to only start listening when prompted with a so-called wake word.

When turned on, Bee devices are always recording. Amazon says this enables key features like conversation summaries and the ability to “review memories from the past few days to remember what you discussed.” It can also track “trends or themes that recur” to give personalized goals or actions.

With a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $12 per month, users can get unlimited conversation summaries and daily memories as well as integrations with Amazon’s webstore, its Alexa+ AI assistant and third-party apps. For example, if a user mentions they need to buy dish soap, they might see the product recommended on the Amazon homepage, or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps.

The company said Bee devices are designed so that “no one, including Amazon, can access your data.” Users can delete their transcripts and summaries at any time and “no audio is ever stored,” Amazon said.

An LED light signals when Bee gadgets are recording, Amazon said.

kept.heading: TELLING AI TO ACT AS YOUR CUSTOMERS MAKES ITS ANSWER WORSE (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI-generated customer personas can overestimate purchase intent and mislead product or campaign decisions. In one test, AI predicted that 52% of shoppers would buy a product when only 33% did. kept.article_text:
Title: Telling AI to act as your customers makes its answer worse: 52% of shoppers would buy, it said. Real sales: 33%.

URL Source: https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/18eDy1

Published Time: 2026-10-17T09:08:51.433Z

Markdown Content:
Ask an AI to pretend to be your customer and it will tend to like your idea more than your customers do. In a pre-registered test against a supermarket's real purchase records, a panel of AI shoppers predicted a 52% purchase rate across five product categories over the next 28 days. The real rate was 33% ([BehaviorLens](https://github.com/meryemsakin/BehaviorLens)). Asked to predict coupon redemptions, the same panel said 32%. The tills said 14%.

I built a product on the opposite bet.

In January 2026 I wrote the plan for PlebTest: AI customer personas that interview you about your idea, push back, and hand down a verdict of kill, pivot or build. It was for founders who dread cold calls, which is me. The landing page promised "brutally honest feedback without picking up the phone". The plan said 1,000 paying founders and $250,000 a year by the end of 2026, with 60% of free trials converting to paid and break-even at three customers ([the planning documents are in the public repo](https://github.com/TheWayWithin/PlebTest)). I had checked none of it with a single real customer. A tool for validating ideas, itself never validated. The README says so now, at the top.

* * *

## What I built

![Image 1: Two panels. Left, the promise in January 2026: brutally honest feedback without picking up the phone, 1,000 paying founders by the end of 2026, 60% of trials converting, break-even at three customers. Right, what shipped: 62 of 78 first-release tasks done, last product commit 10 February 2026, paying customers 0, validated against real customers: never.](https://pub-4f2aa5e351b44f67ba6dd0bc32fe1bb2.r2.dev/blog/ai-fake-customer-interviews-2.png)

_The plan on the left, the record on the right. Both are in the repo._

The engine worked. By 10 February the develop branch had 62 of the 78 tasks for the first release done: sign-in, Stripe billing with pro-rated upgrades, two interview modes, a one-line quick check, and a report that handed down the verdict ([commit history](https://github.com/TheWayWithin/PlebTest/commits/develop)). The part I was proudest of was the anti-sycophancy design. Every panel of personas was 40% high-sceptic, 40% medium, 20% low. The toughest preset, the Critic, had to find at least three objections before showing interest, alongside the Pragmatist and the Cheerleader ([architecture notes](https://github.com/TheWayWithin/PlebTest/blob/develop/architecture.md)). A scorecard counted objections in every session against a minimum of two, and a golden set of test ideas checked the engine wasn't going soft ([project plan](https://github.com/TheWayWithin/PlebTest/blob/develop/project-plan.md)). The spec also said to rerun any reply with too few objections. I never built that part.

Every one of those is a dial. None of them is a reference point. I could make the fake customers harsher or kinder. I had no way of knowing which setting matched real customers, because real customers were the thing the product existed to avoid.

I announced the landing page on LinkedIn on 24 January. The task for launching the product itself, a marketing launch plan, stayed unticked. The last commit to the product was 10 February. I parked it in May, in July I retired the whole model of selling software like this on my own, and the README marks PlebTest killed in August.

* * *

## What the studies say

![Image 2: Two panels from two different studies. Left, supermarket purchases: pretend customers predicted 52%, real households bought 33%; coupons, predicted 32%, redeemed 14%. Right, 399 headline tests: asked plainly, the model's ranking matched real readers at 0.361 and it picked the winner 49.2% of the time; as a persona panel, 0.084 and 34.6%; picking at random, 30.4%.](https://pub-4f2aa5e351b44f67ba6dd0bc32fe1bb2.r2.dev/blog/ai-fake-customer-interviews-3-v2.png)

_Two studies, two different tasks and models. In both, the persona was the weaker method._

Two pre-registered studies from this year put numbers on the thing I'd been tuning by feel.

The first, BehaviorLens (Meryem Sakin, 2026), gave language-model personas a household's shopping history and asked whether it would buy in each of five categories over the next 28 days. That ran across 1,456 household-periods, and every answer was checked against what the household bought. Persona panel: 52% predicted, 33% observed. Coupons: 32% predicted, 14% redeemed. The models were also asked to rank nine coupon campaigns by how many people would redeem them, scored on rank agreement, where 1 is a perfect match and 0 is no better than chance. A gradient-boosting model, the standard machine-learning tool for this, built on the same data, scored 0.55. A language model given the same structured data and no persona scored 0.13. The persona panel scored minus 0.10. The author's own caveats: nine campaigns is nine data points, the dataset is public so the models may have seen it in training, each question was asked once, and only one persona design was tested.

The second (Alexandre Maiorano, 2026) took the 399 of 1,695 headline A/B tests in the Upworthy archive that had a clear winner, where real readers on real traffic picked it by clicking. Asking the model which headline a typical reader would click, with no further persona, matched the real ranking at 0.361 and picked the winner 49.2% of the time. A panel of ten personas built from real audience demographics scored 0.084 and 34.6%. Picking at random gets 30.4% ([arXiv 2609.25010](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25010)). His explanation: asked plainly, the model draws on an accurate sense of what people in general do. Told to play a particular person, it adds bias and noise.

I'd built the persona layer as the feature. In both studies it was the part that made the answer worse.

Both of those panels were built from real data: each household's own shopping record, or published demographics of the real audience. The persona a founder writes from a guess about their customer has less to go on.

* * *

## Why the sceptic dial could not fix it

![Image 3: A chain of four steps. Ask the model plainly: the best predictor in the headline study. Give it a persona: adds bias and noise, the ranking falls from 0.361 to 0.084. Turn up the scepticism: moves the answer, in a direction I chose. Check it against real customers: one correction method needs 50 to 300 real answers, and I had none.](https://pub-4f2aa5e351b44f67ba6dd0bc32fe1bb2.r2.dev/blog/ai-fake-customer-interviews-4-v2.png)

_Each step after the first made the answer different. None made it checkable._

My instinct was that the trouble with AI customers is that they're too nice, so the fix is to make them meaner. The BehaviorLens result agrees the panel was too nice, so a meaner panel might well land closer. The trouble is knowing how much closer, or when it has gone past. A dial that adds objections moves the answer by an amount I chose, with nothing real to check it against.

BehaviorLens shows what a real reference point does. Calibrated on a held-back slice of the real purchase data, the persona panel's extra error over the no-persona model fell from 0.0550 to 0.0049 on its accuracy score, about nine tenths of the gap gone. The fix for a fake customer is real customers.

Tigre and Souto (2026) ask when you can trust a synthetic consumer panel as it is, when you can correct it, and when you should abandon it. Their correction method needs a sample of 50 to 300 real responses to calibrate against. And once you have that sample, their own figures show the real answers on their own are more precise than the corrected panel ([arXiv 2609.13148](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13148)). A founder who uses an AI panel to avoid talking to 50 people has exactly the data needed to calibrate it: none.

Simile, which sells simulated users for marketing and product research, raised $200 million at a $2 billion valuation on 30 July 2026 ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/?p=3148353)). I don't think that contradicts the studies. A buyer with real customer data can, in principle, calibrate a panel against it. The product I built was for the one buyer who has nothing to calibrate with.

* * *

## What a fake customer is still good for

![Image 4: A card listing four uses. Three hold up: finding the objection you haven't thought of, then asking real people what they did; rehearsing the conversation; comparing two versions with no persona. One doesn't: the kill, pivot or build verdict.](https://pub-4f2aa5e351b44f67ba6dd0bc32fe1bb2.r2.dev/blog/ai-fake-customer-interviews-5-v2.png)

_Keep the first three. The fourth was the product._

I'd use one again for three things, and never for the fourth.

1.   **Finding the objection you haven't thought of.** My own sample card had a persona called Sarah saying "I already use Rover. Unless you're half the price, I'm not switching." As a reminder that the question exists, that's free and instant. Whether real dog owners would say it is a separate question the persona can't answer. So turn it into a question for a real person about what they did: how did you find your dog walker, and have you ever switched?
2.   **Rehearsing the conversation.** If you're going to talk to real people and the prospect scares you, a few rounds with a rude persona takes the edge off. Practise asking what people did, not pitching. That's practice, not evidence.
3.   **Comparing versions, with no persona.** The headline study's win was a comparison: give the model two or more versions of the same thing and ask which a typical customer would pick. Two prices, two opening lines, two ways of describing the problem. Don't ask it whether people would buy at all. That's a level, and the level is what the personas got wrong.

The fourth is the verdict. Kill, pivot or build was the product's whole promise. None of the three studies tested a verdict like that, but every verdict rests on a guess about how many people would buy, and that guess is the number the personas got wrong, in the kind direction.

What replaces it is the step the product was built to skip: a few conversations with real people about what they did, not what they would do. PlebTest's own plan had a task for exactly that, a minimum real-world validation plan. It was never built.

The evidence is narrow. BehaviorLens tested purchase forecasting at one retailer. Maiorano tested headline ranking, and the gap was small on a second news dataset and vanished on Reddit titles. Tigre and Souto tested population estimates. None of them tested an interview about an unbuilt product. If someone publishes a pre-registered test where persona panels beat the plain question on real purchase data, I'll change my mind and say so here.

The repo is public under an MIT licence. The engine runs. The verdict screen still says kill, pivot or build in large type. The studies say to read everything on that screen except the verdict.

* * *

## Sources

*   Sakin, M. (2026). BehaviorLens: a pre-registered evaluation of LLM personas against held-out dunnhumby retail transactions. [https://github.com/meryemsakin/BehaviorLens](https://github.com/meryemsakin/BehaviorLens)
*   Maiorano, A. C. (2026). Do Synthetic Personas Predict Real Audience Response? A Sim-to-Real Study Where a No-Persona Baseline Beats Persona-Based Copy Simulation. arXiv:2609.25010. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25010](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25010)
*   Tigre, R. and Gobato Souto, H. (2026). When Can You Trust Your Synthetic Users? Diagnostics and Corrections for LLM Consumer Panels. arXiv:2609.13148. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13148](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13148)
*   TechCrunch, 30 July 2026. Synthetic-user startup Simile raises $200M at $2B valuation 5 months after $100M Series A. [https://techcrunch.com/?p=3148353](https://techcrunch.com/?p=3148353)
*   PlebTest repository, planning documents, architecture, project plan and commit history. [https://github.com/TheWayWithin/PlebTest](https://github.com/TheWayWithin/PlebTest)

Title: Gated Content Is the #1 Enemy of AI Search

URL Source: https://marketingadvice.substack.com/p/gated-content-is-the-1-enemy-of-ai

Published Time: 2026-10-14T12:45:50+00:00

Markdown Content:
*   **Gated content and AI search are fundamentally at odds with each other:**because they rely on completely opposing philosophies regarding how content gets distributed and how value gets captured.

*   **AI search prioritizes “zero-click” frictionless answer delivery:**LLMs want content pages that are crawlable, indexable and extractable.

*   **Gated content remains locked behind lead-capture forms or paywalls:**therefore gated assets are invisible to AI crawlers like OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, etc.

*   **LLMs cannot fill out lead-capture forms or bypass paywalls.**They may only retrieve “splash pages” with teaser content, which generally don’t offer much value.

*   **Gated assets get excluded from both AI training datasets and real-time LLM retrieval systems:**Examples would be things like PDFs, white papers, on-demand webinars and analyst reports.

*   **B2B companies are doing this because they want MQLs:**They would rather drive MQLs at the top of the funnel with gated content assets, instead of maximizing brand authority and visibility in AI-generated responses with ungated content.

*   **The problem is that MQLs have horrible conversion rates to sales opps:**Every marketer knows this, yet for some reason, the hamster wheel continues.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Gl-u!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb0fe0df2-995f-4a3e-bcbb-b8c2b3d10ef5_1672x941.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Gl-u!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb0fe0df2-995f-4a3e-bcbb-b8c2b3d10ef5_1672x941.png)

I’ve worked with over a dozen B2B SaaS companies in the past year, and all of them are prioritizing GEO as a top strategic initiative.

Executives want to know why ChatGPT isn’t recommending them, why competitors keep showing up in Claude, and why their brand isn’t mentioned in AI overviews.

**At the same time, some of their best content assets are locked behind a form.**

Therefore, gated content is counterproductive to AEO being a top strategic initiative.

*   **Definition:** High-value assets accessible only after filling out a form.

*   **Typical Formats:** Original research reports, eBooks, whitepapers, live webinars, product demos, and exclusive newsletters.

*   **Benefits:**

    *   **MQL Lead Generation:** Direct access to target prospect email inboxes to fuel lead nurturing sequences.

    *   **Audience Segmentation:** Topic downloads reveal specific prospect pain points, allowing for tailored outreach and email automation.

    *   **Intent Filtering:** Filters out casual visitors, leaving higher-intent prospects willing to trade personal data for insights.

    *   **Exclusivity:** Creates a premium perception if the material is genuinely unique.

*   **Drawbacks:**

    *   **SEO & AI Search Invisibility:** Search engine bots and LLM crawlers cannot crawl or index content behind forms, eliminating organic search traffic and backlink opportunities.

    *   **Drives Hordes of Unqualified Leads:** Most people don’t want to talk to sales, they just want to check out a content asset.

    *   **High Friction:** Increases bounce rates and leads to form fatigue or fake contact submissions.

    *   **PDF Cannibalization:** Indexable hosted PDFs (e.g., uploaded via HubSpot) may cannibalize and outrank main HTML web pages.

*   **Definition:** Content freely accessible on the web without form submissions or paywalls.

*   **Typical Formats:** Blog posts, videos, podcasts, infographics, ungated PDFs, landing pages, and open research articles.

*   **Benefits:**

    *   **Organic Growth & SEO:** Crawlable by search engines, generating multi-year compounding traffic and earning authoritative backlinks.

    *   **AI Search Visibility:** Immediately retrievable by AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity) for vendor recommendations and citations.

    *   **Virality & Distribution:** Acquires backlinks, drives brand awareness and social sharing across channels.

*   **Drawbacks:**

    *   **Does Not Generate MQLs:** Visitors can consume insights without providing their contact details.

    *   **Funnel Tracking Gaps:** Harder to map individual buyer journeys prior to direct hand-raising.

Buyers are relying on AI systems to research categories, compare vendors, and form their vendor shortlists before they ever speak to sales.

Hiding your best information doesn’t just cost you traffic. **[It limits your ability to influence the answer](https://lnkd.in/p/e7YJ-nhG).**

When a crawler from OpenAI or Anthropic hits your gated landing page, it reads the headline, maybe a brief summary paragraph, and then it hits a wall.

The actual meat of your content—the methodology, the data points, the expert interviews, the unique point of view—is locked inside a PDF on the other side of that wall.

This creates a massive problem for your brand’s discoverability:

AI search needs useful, accessible information to build an answer. Original data, proprietary research, benchmark findings, and distinct analysis give these systems something they can’t get from another generic category explainer. When all of that sits behind a form, you’re making your most differentiated expertise harder to retrieve and reference.

Searchers are getting instant, synthesized answers from AI engines without ever clicking a blue link. If an AI model cannot access your data to formulate its answer, you lose the zero-click battle. The AI will simply synthesize the answer using your competitor’s ungated content instead, giving them the citation and the brand authority.

In the modern buying journey, a prospect asks an LLM for a list of vendors or a solution to a problem. The LLM recommends a brand. The prospect then opens a new tab, goes directly to that brand’s homepage, and converts. If your best content is invisible to the AI, you never even make it into the picture.

For years, running the gated content playbook for MQL generation was the “bread and butter” of enterprise demand generation.

You created a high-value asset. You put it behind a form. A prospect gives you their contact info, your CRM logs an MQL, and an SDR follows up. It was a predictable machine for gauging prospect intent and providing sales teams with “leads” to chase down.

Gated content downloads are still the gold standard for most enterprise demand gen programs. It’s trackable, reportable, and directly attributable.

But even before AI entered the picture, the MQL gated asset model was starting to crack.

**[B2B buyers increasingly want to research vendors anonymously](https://searchengineland.com/the-dark-seo-funnel-why-traffic-no-longer-proves-seo-success-470334).** They know that filling out a form means subjecting themselves to an automated email sequence and an incoming cold call. Because of this friction, gated landing pages may drive MQLs but it’s largely a batch of leads that aren’t interested.

*   **Why un-gate?** Hard gating **[hides information](https://searchengineland.com/gating-ai-hide-show-why-461535)** from search engines and AI crawlers, reducing organic discoverability, AI search citations, and market education.

*   **When to gate?** Hard gating should be reserved exclusively for high-value, proprietary, personalized, licensed, or sales-assisted assets where the value exchange is beneficial to the buyer.

*   **Is this commodity content?**Be honest about what you’re gating. If it’s highly commoditized information that LLMs can easily answer on their own, then don’t gate.

When gating, marketers need to consider the value exchange from the buyer’s perspective (and the AI crawler’s perspective).

In the AI search era, **you have to earn the right to ask for an email address.**

In other words, you should only gate assets that are truly exclusive, rare and high value.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PiYq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3ca881d1-c879-4ae2-8e36-5bdf75865e40_1896x1262.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PiYq!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3ca881d1-c879-4ae2-8e36-5bdf75865e40_1896x1262.png)

Historically, B2B SaaS companies have over-gated mid-funnel assets like commercial playbooks, use-case breakdowns, and pricing context.

**If content helps buyers understand your category, evaluate your product, or choose you over a competitor, keep it public.** Don’t make someone fill out a form just to understand why they should buy from you.

*   **Comparisons and buyer’s guides:**Your brand vs. competitors, alternatives, and evaluation criteria.

*   **Product and use-case pages:**Capabilities, workflows, industry applications, and recorded demos.

*   **Pricing context:**Plans, packaging, cost drivers, and implementation expenses.

*   **Technical information:**Integrations, deployment requirements, migration guides, and security overviews.

*   **Case studies:**Customer problems, solutions, and measurable results.

*   **Research findings:** Original data, key takeaways, and methodology—even if the full research package is gated.

*   **Category explanations and FAQs:** Basic questions shouldn’t require a work email.

*   **Playbooks and how-to guides:**Advice that helps buyers solve problems and understand your approach.

If you are publishing resource-intensive assets like original research, benchmark data, or comprehensive industry reports, you may be able to effectively balance discoverability with lead capture.

Say your company has produced an impressive and proprietary benchmark report, such as **[Jellyfish’s 2026 state of engineering management report](https://jellyfish.co/2026-state-of-engineering-management/)**.

Instead of locking the entire asset behind a form, you can build a comprehensive, ungated landing page that acts as the hub for your research. Publish your executive summary, your methodology, your boldest takeaways, and your most compelling charts openly on this page so AI bots can read and cite your data.

Offer the full PDF download, the extended bonus materials, or the raw datasets behind a form for those who are highly engaged and want the deep dive. This gives search engines and AI crawlers the core value of the page (and stats to cite), while still offering a conversion path for highly engaged visitors.

Hard gates should only be used for highly tactical assets where the value exchange overwhelmingly favors the buyer.

**Content Types:**

*   Licensed third-party analyst reports

*   Personalized ROI audits

*   Private calculators

*   Highly proprietary resources

The emphasis should be placed on licensed third-party analyst reports (like Gartner or Forrester), personalized ROI audits, private calculators, or detailed implementation scripts.

One example of this would be **[OutSystems’ Gartner Magic Quadrant](https://www.outsystems.com/1/low-code-application-platforms-gartner)** recognition for enterprise low-code application platforms.

Third-party reports often require a gate due to syndication rules anyway, and they offer objective, external validation that buyers would gladly trade an email for.

Treat these assets like premium digital products. If the value is undeniable, buyers will fill out the form without remorse. And make sure your sales team doesn’t spam them either!

*   **Prevent PDF Cannibalization:** Set all hosted PDF copies of website guides to **noindex** in your CMS to ensure search engines rank the main web page rather than the PDF asset.

*   **Noindex Splash Pages:** Ensure active gated landing pages carry a **noindex** tag so they do not compete with or cannibalize organic HTML pillar pages.

*   **Hybrid Publishing Strategy:** Prioritize on-page optimized HTML pillar pages for SEO and LLM indexing, while repurposing existing gated assets into modular web content.

The era of holding basic educational content hostage in exchange for an email address is over.

AI search has fundamentally changed how B2B buyers discover, research, and evaluate software. If you continue to optimize for old MQL metrics by putting paywalls in front of your best content, you are actively choosing to be invisible.

The formula going forward is simple: remove the friction from the research process. Let your data speak for itself, build trust through transparency, and only ask for contact information when the value exchange is greater for the buyer than it is for the marketing team.

Title: Your next marketing hire should probably surprise you

URL Source: https://www.kieranflanagan.io/p/your-next-marketing-hire-should-probably

Published Time: 2026-10-16T11:13:34+00:00

Markdown Content:
I’ve hired hundreds of marketers and growth professionals. Great leaders excel at hiring. It’s not just about sourcing, interviewing, or hiring. It’s about staying ahead of the curve on the skills you hire for.

A lot of the job descriptions I’ve used would need rewriting today.

Look at who Ramp brought into a marketing brainstorm: someone who had spent four years leading social for MrBeast. They ended up putting Brian Baumgartner, Kevin from _The Office_, in a glass box in New York doing expense reports.

ClickUp pays comedians and outside creators to join its writers’ rooms and improve its scripts.

These are software companies recruiting people who understand entertainment.

In 2021, I led HubSpot’s acquisition of The Hustle because we saw this trend. Make relevant content, not just educational.

Now, AI has commoditized so much of what we used to do. It can produce an infinite number of articles, videos, and campaigns. Your competitors have access to the same tools—the same models. You don’t even need to be a great prompter to get AI to produce pretty good results.

AI is commoditizing the consideration phase. And that changes where I’d spend my hiring budget.

I’d want people who can make our product interesting enough to watch. People who understand what our customers send to their friends. People who can convince creators with great audiences to build something with us.

When marketing moved to digital, everything became more professional. Optimized to the very last metric. It lost its edge, soul, and personality.

The battle is now in the awareness stage. To win, I’d make these three roles a critical part of my team.

_Quick note: I’m going to be posting every two weeks for the rest of this year. I took on some new things. Became a best selling author. And finally reached 100k subs on YouTube. In doing all that, I need to fix my workload and I want to ensure quality is very high._

**1. Viral Producer**

**What is it?**

Someone who runs experiments that get us known. That help us win the stage above consideration → Awareness.

They take a problem our product solves and turn it into something people want to watch, participate in, or talk about. They own getting the idea made, getting it distributed, and deciding whether it deserves another investment.

**Why now?**

In PLG businesses, we built strong experimentation teams around sign-ups, activation, and conversion. I want that same discipline applied earlier, to awareness.

As buyers do more of their research inside AI assistants, I think being familiar before they start comparing products becomes more critical.

At the same time, AI makes parts of creative production cheaper. We can test more concepts before committing to a big production. That creates room for someone who combines a growth operator’s appetite for experiments with a producer’s ability to make things people care about.

**Example**

Ramp sells finance software. They put Kevin from _The Office_ in a glass box in New York and made him process receipts by hand while a tracker compared him with Ramp.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pjjW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc3391771-2a85-47ef-8d6e-04ff27ed6b49_1532x1066.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pjjW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc3391771-2a85-47ef-8d6e-04ff27ed6b49_1532x1066.png)

**[[Brian video here]](https://youtu.be/b26ckd9AhsQ?si=2m3ewZrUBzFYK0N7)**

Then came a partnership with Kumar, a retired-accountant character whose finance videos look like thriller trailers. And a Broadway musical about paying bills, starring Billy Porter.

This is the range of work I mean by a Viral Producer.

**How it works**

Ramp has a dedicated **Creative Experimentation team reporting into growth marketing**. Its current roster includes:

*   **Kendall Tucker, Director of Creative Experimentation.**

*   **Three senior creative producers:** Amber Layne, Mads Montana and Nolan Lunsford. Their backgrounds include acting, comedy, dance and YouTube entertainment.

*   **Dallas Thompson, Influencer Manager.**

*   **Robert Lipman, Visibility Engineer.**

*   A rotating group of freelance producers, directors, comedians and other talent.

The team owns the idea, execution and clips, and measures views, shares and downstream impact.

**2. Internet Comedian**

**What is it?**

Someone who makes your brand something customers send to their friends.

That could mean memes, short sketches, recurring characters, or an AI remix of a trend. They understand internet culture.

**Why now?**

Social is the new SEO

In the inbound era, you scaled via keywords and content. Now, you scale through memes and shit posting.

Basically, you have to be relevant online. The early-stage founders I speak with, pre-seed, seed, and series A, are more marketing than engineering. And they understand you need to do things differently online.

Check out this from a company called Monid.ai, whose co-founder Shengkun I met earlier this week. Their product is great. Their marketing is also great.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_3wL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe547c243-3af9-43ac-809e-9d08fe798c25_1536x2048.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_3wL!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe547c243-3af9-43ac-809e-9d08fe798c25_1536x2048.jpeg)

AI gives that person more ways to execute. They can mock up a character, edit a clip, or try several versions quickly. The valuable skill is having taste and judgment to know what would be funny in the first place.

And we’ve done this before. In 1957, Jim Henson was making puppet commercials for Wilkins Coffee. In one, a puppet refuses the coffee and gets shot with a cannon. [Watch it here](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%22Cannon%22_Wilkins_Coffee_commercial_(1957).webm).

Imagine getting that through your brand review today. We’ve lost our edge.

We have better production tools than ever, and so much B2B marketing still sounds like a corporate induction.

**Example**

Look at how Alexandr Wang promoted Muse.

Meta’s chief AI officer turned its fluffy mascot into material for memes, pop-culture references and jokes about competitors. Business Insider counted more than 300 posts on X between Muse’s launch on September 8 and its September 23 report. [Source](https://www.businessinsider.tw/article/7476)

When someone complimented his social team, Wang said he was posting himself:

> “I don’t let the corposlops near my tweet cannon.” [Source](https://www.axios.com/2026/09/25/ai-doom-meta-muse-mascot)

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9CV7!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc06ca134-df68-4da2-bdeb-d4b65cd43fc6_599x579.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9CV7!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc06ca134-df68-4da2-bdeb-d4b65cd43fc6_599x579.jpeg)

That’s the instinct you need in an Internet Comedian. Someone who sees what people are already laughing about and knows how to put our product into the joke. Obviously Alex Wang is much more than an internet comedian lol

ClickUp has built a more formal process around this. It pays comedians and outside creators to join writers’ rooms, bring ideas, and improve scripts.

**How it works**

This is simple: you either can do this content or you can’t. You either have this skill in-house, or you don’t.

Hire a comedic script writer. Do a contract to try it out. Look for young, out-of-college grads who understand how to create content people share.

Pay a comedy writer or creator to turn those observations into five premises. Produce a few simple versions before commissioning anything expensive.

**3. Creator Deal Maker**

**What is it?**

Someone who makes the creators your customers follow want to work with you.

They find the right talent, understand what those creators want to build and put together an offer worth accepting.

**Why now?**

If a creator is a good fit for your company, they’re probably a good fit for several others.

You need a reason for them to choose you and stay. That might include money, production support, access, distribution or a project they couldn’t easily make alone.

This takes commercial judgement and relationship skills. A standard sponsorship email only gets you so far.

**Example**

At HubSpot, one of the things we did in our creator programme was cross-promote the creators.

Being part of the programme helped them grow their own audiences. We had something valuable to offer beyond the sponsorship fee, and a reason for them to keep participating.

We also bought half their ad inventory for 2 years, locking them into long-term deals meant they had predictability on their revenue, and we got the upside on their audience growth as we had locked in the CPM cost. For example, one of our creators grew their audience 5x during those 2 years, and that was all free visibility for us.

That’s the kind of deal I’d want this person to figure out: what can we offer that becomes more valuable the longer we work together?

**How it works**

First, check who actually engages with the creator. Look at relevant job roles, markets and the quality of the conversations.

I built a creator grader to help with this. In one case, roughly 80% of the engaging profiles I examined had no connections and looked newly created. That was a reason to investigate before paying. A big engagement number can hide a poor audience.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!V0R3!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F714a64ba-54d6-4270-b010-aaed00036891_2880x2830.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!V0R3!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F714a64ba-54d6-4270-b010-aaed00036891_2880x2830.png)

Then ask what the creator wants to build. Match that ambition with something your company can genuinely provide.

Start with a paid three-part pilot. Agree the fee, creative control, usage rights and what would justify continuing.

I’d look for someone who can explain both sides of the deal: why it works for our business, and why the creator would choose it over another offer.

Before opening your next marketing role, put a small budget behind one of these experiments.

Commission an entertaining product concept. Bring a comedian into a writing session. Build an offer for a creator you’d love to work with.

You’ll learn far more about the skills your team is missing by making something together than by rewriting the same job description you used last year.

Until Next Time,

Happy AI;fying

Published Time: Wed, 10 Sep 2025 21:05:01 GMT

Markdown Content:
Can't attend? Sign up anyway to be sent the recording.

**From Inside Reddit to Inside HubSpot: What It Actually Takes to Win on Reddit**

Evan Hamilton spent five years inside Reddit, looking after the volunteer moderators who run its communities. Then he crossed to the brand side and had to make Reddit work for HubSpot.

Even with all that insider knowledge, plenty of it didn't work first time.

Most brands are now being told Reddit is the key to showing up in AI search. Cue a wave of agencies promising to "game" it with volume. Evan has seen exactly how that ends. He's built HubSpot's presence the other way: replying before posting, earning trust with moderators, finding the customers who'll talk about you better than you ever could, and treating it all as an experiment rather than a playbook.

Join Evan Hamilton, Director of Community at HubSpot and former community lead at Reddit, in conversation with Rob Fawkes from Standing on Giants. They'll talk about what winning on Reddit really looks like for a B2B brand, and what any company can take from it.

**What we'll cover:**

*   What Evan learned about moderators and subreddit culture from inside Reddit, and what most brands still get wrong

*   How HubSpot proved Reddit works for B2B, including the tactics that flopped along the way

*   Brand accounts, personal accounts, and finding the customers and employees who will speak for you

*   Reddit, LLMs and AI search: where the real opportunity is, and why the shortcuts backfire

*   Live Q&A with Evan

**Who this is for:** Brand, marketing and product leaders, B2B included, who know Reddit matters for visibility but want to get it right rather than get banned.

**About the Speakers**

Evan Hamilton was most recently Director of Community at HubSpot, where he built community experiences that drive customer engagement and retention. Before HubSpot, he spent five years leading community at Reddit, setting the strategy that supported tens of thousands of volunteer moderators running hundreds of thousands of communities. He's been bringing people together professionally for over 20 years, with stints at Nextdoor, CMX, UserVoice and more. Outside work he makes music, and he co-founded International Beer Day, which grew from an idea between friends into events around the world.

Rob Fawkes heads up Client Partnerships at Standing on Giants. Standing on Giants helps brands tap into the human-powered internet on Reddit, Discord, forums and social. It's 100% employee-owned and B Corp-certified, and for fifteen years it has worked with brands like Airbnb, Lenovo and Sonos. Rob leads the charge on Reddit, a platform he's genuinely a bit obsessed with. He's a firm believer that the best way onto Reddit is the slow way: building actual relationships with moderators and communities rather than parachuting in with a brand voice nobody asked for.
