Title: How to Automate Content Creation: A Follow-Along Guide

URL Source: https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/

Published Time: 2026-10-16T09:21:11+00:00

Markdown Content:
Automated content creation is the use of software or AI to complete a repeatable sequence of content-production tasks.

When people hear “automated content creation”, I imagine they picture something like this: Enter a keyword, click a button, and poof! An article is made. From there, they’ll generate 500 articles before the day ends and publish all of them.

I don’t want to say these systems don’t exist. They do. In fact, we’ve [even made one](https://ahrefs.com/blog/how-i-do-content-engineering-with-claude-code/). But our content cadence has remained the same.

Because it’s not our goal at Ahrefs to contribute even more spam and [slop](https://ahrefs.com/blog/how-we-use-ai-without-making-ai-slop/) to the Internet.

Yes, we want to make more content. But we want to make more **useful** content. More _better_ content. Not simply more content.

Automation can help: not by replacing the interesting parts of content marketing, but by freeing us from the boring ones.

Because I love making content that helps people and promotes our brand. But let’s be real: Not every part of content marketing is equally enjoyable. Some parts are really, really, really boring. Unfortunately, they’re also important.

Take updating content.

Google loves [fresh content](https://ahrefs.com/blog/fresh-content/). When its Query Deserves Freshness (QDF) algorithm detects that a topic needs current information, it boosts recently updated pages. Likewise for AI assistants. [Our study found that](https://ahrefs.com/blog/do-ai-assistants-prefer-to-cite-fresh-content/) compared to traditional search results, AI assistants prefer citing fresher content.

Updating is easy enough when you have one article. Not so easy when you have dozens. Or hundreds.

That was the problem I had. Over the years, I’d created a collection of data-driven articles like our [top Google searches](https://ahrefs.com/blog/top-google-searches/) and [most searched questions](https://ahrefs.com/blog/top-google-questions/). Having to update all of them was a giant chore.

So I built something I call the **Data Refresh Hub**.

Every month, it:

*   Pulls fresh data for 12 datasets
*   Removes NSFW results and makes sure it fits the category (e.g., questions for “top Google questions”)
*   Rebuilds the relevant tables and charts
*   Updates our WordPress drafts
*   Emails me when it’s finished
*   Waits for me to review everything before anything gets published

In other words, the machine now does most of the boring work.

This guide will show you how I built it and, more importantly, how you can apply the same process to the annoying content tasks you wish would disappear from your own to-do list.

Contents

*   [What you’ll need to follow along](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#what-youll-need-to-follow-along)
*   [1. Choose one repeatable content job](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#1-choose-one-repeatable-content-job)
*   [2. Write down exactly how you make it](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#2-write-down-exactly-how-you-make-it)
*   [3. Give the system the information it needs](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#3-give-the-system-the-information-it-needs)
*   [4. Show it what good and bad look like](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#4-show-it-what-good-and-bad-look-like)
*   [5. Make one piece from start to finish](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#5-make-one-piece-from-start-to-finish)
*   [6. Run it for real, then put it on a schedule](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#6-run-it-for-real-then-put-it-on-a-schedule)
*   [7. Scale it up](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#7-scale-it-up)
*   [What still goes wrong with my workflow](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#what-still-goes-wrong-with-my-workflow)
*   [Final thoughts](https://ahrefs.com/blog/automated-content-creation/#final-thoughts)

## What you’ll need to follow along

If you want to build your own automation while reading this guide, you’ll need a few things:

*   One content job you already perform repeatedly, like my monthly updates of “top Google searches”
*   An example of a finished result you consider good, e.g., the data tables in “top Google searches”
*   Access to the information needed to produce it, e.g., Keywords Explorer
*   Somewhere to send the finished draft, e.g., WordPress
*   An AI agent or automation tool capable of connecting everything together, e.g., [Letaido](https://letaido.com/)

Don’t worry if you don’t have all of these yet. Part of this guide is figuring them out.

You will, however, need to decide which AI agent or automation platform you want to use.

I chose [Letaido](https://letaido.com/) because it had everything I needed in one place:

*   Complete access to Ahrefs data
*   Ability to switch between models (e.g., Opus 5.5, GPT-Sol 5.6, GPT-Sol 6)
*   Workflows that could be shared with the rest of the team (if the automation was successful, then others in the team could potentially use it too)
*   Complicated developer stuff like hosting and secrets handled for me
*   Connectors to platforms like WordPress

The last point was important for me because I didn’t want to build an automation that did 90% of the work, only for me to spend the final 10% copying tables from one tool and pasting them into WordPress every month. Which defeats the purpose.

You can, of course, use your favorite agent instead. Claude Code, Codex, or whatever else you prefer.

You may just have to do some extra work connecting [MCPs](https://ahrefs.com/seo-mcp), WordPress, databases, or whatever other systems your workflow depends on.

## 1. Choose one repeatable content job

Don’t start by asking: How can we use AI?

I think this is where a lot of companies go wrong. The question is so open-ended that you end up staring into an infinite universe of possibilities. And when there are infinite possibilities, people don’t necessarily dream bigger.

They get a headache.

Then they go back to whatever they were already doing. Instead, start with your biggest existing frustration.

**What is something you already have to do that you wish you didn’t?**

If nothing immediately comes to mind, list the work that happens every week, month, quarter, or every time a piece of content gets produced.

Then look for tasks that are:

*   **Repetitive**, e.g., you have to do it every day, week, or month
*   **Time-consuming**, e.g., it takes more time than you expect each time
*   **Governed by reasonably stable rules**, e.g., keyword research, where the process is mostly the same no matter the industry
*   **Valuable when done correctly**, e.g., it has [business potential](https://ahrefs.com/blog/brew-framework/)
*   **Frequently delayed, rushed, or skipped**, e.g., it takes more time than usual so you procrastinate

For me, one obvious candidate was updating our data-driven articles.

These articles were most useful when the numbers were current. They also tended to get the most search traffic when we updated them.

But every refresh required me to:

*   Pull new data from multiple places
*   Remove irrelevant results
*   Check the figures for mistakes
*   Build new tables and charts
*   Rewrite parts of the post if something important had changed
*   Change titles or subheadings where necessary
*   Update the publication date

If I had one article, this would have been fine. But the collection kept growing.

Eventually, updating everything monthly became unsustainable. So we compromised and moved to quarterly updates, even though monthly would have been better for readers.

## 2. Write down exactly how you make it

An agent cannot reliably automate a process that nobody can explain.

This sounds obvious. It isn't. Most of us do repeat tasks on autopilot, and autopilot is terrible at explaining itself.

So before you build anything, reconstruct how you actually do the job. I don't mean how you think you do it, or how it's written in an SOP nobody has opened in years. I mean how you really do it, including the shortcuts.

Record every meaningful action. That includes the small things and the corrections that are easy to forget.

Here's roughly what my process for updating Top Google Searches looked like once I wrote it all down:

*   Go to [Keywords Explorer](https://ahrefs.com/keywords-explorer) and do an empty search with the country filter set to the U.S.
*   Download the CSV for the top 200 keywords
*   Open the CSV, check the list, and remove anything that doesn’t seem right (e.g., NSFW queries)
*   Spot-check the top results against last month's to catch anything that looks off
*   Round all numbers up to the nearest 10,000.
*   Copy-paste the data into TablePress, the plugin that hosts all our tables
*   Make sure nothing went awry
*   Go to an internal tool and pull the queries for top global Google searches
*   Rinse and repeat the above process for these set of keywords
*   Check whether the changes are big enough to warrant rewriting the intro or subheadings
*   Make sure all images in the blog post are up-to-date
*   Update the "last updated" date

As you can see, there are a lot of little decisions here and there that you likely won’t remember off the top of your head because it comes so naturally to you. Writing them down is how you find them.

A pro tip I can give you is to ask the agent to interview you.

Try something like:

`I want to automate [task]. Interview me about how I currently do it, one question at a time. Whenever my answer is vague or I say "usually," "it depends," or "I just know," ask a follow-up question. At the end, write up the full process as a step-by-step checklist, including every rule and exception I mentioned.`
You’ll probably discover you have a lot more unwritten rules than you thought.

Once you have that checklist, don’t leave it sitting in a doc. Turn it into a skill file: a saved set of instructions your agent follows every time it runs the job, so you write the process down once and never have to re-explain it. I’ve covered how to build one in [our guide to Claude Skills](https://ahrefs.com/blog/claude-skills/).

## 3. Give the system the information it needs

I wouldn’t rely on an LLM’s memory or generic web search for information that matters to your workflow.

LLMs are known to make up numbers and web search tends to pull from whatever it finds. That could be a listicle from five years ago or even AI slop. Hardly worth trusting.

You want to tell the LLM which sources it should use. Then connect those sources to it, whether through an MCP, an API, or uploaded files.

Depending on what you’re creating, that might include:

*   **First-party data**, e.g., data generated by your company or from your products
*   **APIs**, e.g., connections to other tools or data sources you use
*   **Product documentation**, e.g., your internal product documentation or help centre
*   **Customer interviews**
*   **Approved research**, e.g., your company only cites or quotes from reputable sources or academic journals
*   **Existing articles**, e.g., your blog or YouTube channel
*   **Search data**, e.g., data from Ahrefs
*   **Editorial guidelines**

Connect your agent to Ahrefs with the Ahrefs MCP

* * *

If your workflow runs on search data, the [Ahrefs MCP server](https://ahrefs.com/seo-mcp) lets Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, and other AI tools pull live data straight from your Ahrefs account. It’s hosted by Ahrefs, so there’s nothing to install.

Connect your account and your agent can query Keywords Explorer, Site Explorer, and more from the chat.

For my Data Refresh Hub, different articles require different sources. Here’s where everything came from:

| Dataset | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Top Google Searches, Top Google Questions, Trending Topics, Most Expensive Keywords | [Keywords Explorer](https://ahrefs.com/keywords-explorer) |
| Most Cited Domains | [Brand Radar](https://ahrefs.com/brand-radar) |
| Most Searched People | [Keywords Explorer](https://ahrefs.com/keywords-explorer) + LLM magic (more on this below) |
| Global tables in Top Google Searches and Top Google Questions | Ahrefs' internal database |

The rule of thumb: the LLM's job is to process the data, not to be the data.

## 4. Show it what good and bad look like

Instructions are useful. Examples are better.

If your workflow involves judgment calls, give the system examples of:

*   Things you would accept
*   Things you would reject
*   Why you made each decision
*   Ambiguous cases that should go to a human

Your goal is to turn recurring editorial decisions into explicit rules.

For example, Top Google Questions is supposed to be a list of, well, questions. The simplest rule would be "keep anything that starts with who, what, where, when, why, or how."

Sounds simple. Except lots of queries start with a question word and aren't questions at all:

*   **How to Train Your Dragon:** a movie
*   **How I Met Your Mother:** a TV series
*   **Would you rather questions:** a _category_ of questions, not a question

Sometimes the LLM won't catch these right away. It sees "how" at the start and a sensible-looking phrase after it. A human (me) needs to tell it explicitly why these shouldn't be accepted.

Fortunately for me, Letaido was capable enough to spot it:

This is where the reasons matter. If I only say "reject How to Train Your Dragon," the model learns one exception. If I say "reject titles of movies, TV shows, books, and songs, even when they're phrased as questions," it learns a rule. Now it can also catch something like How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days without me ever mentioning it.

Most Searched People had a different problem.

This one was harder, because we don't have that data in Ahrefs. There's no ready-made list of "people" to pull from. So I needed the LLM to analyze the data we do have and pull out the entities that belong to a person.

That's harder than it sounds. Is "Jordan" a basketball player, a country, or a pair of sneakers? Should "Taylor Swift tickets" count toward Taylor Swift?

Use Ahrefs’ entity filters for ambiguous names

* * *

Telling a person apart from a product or a place is exactly what our entity filters are built for. In [Brand Radar](https://ahrefs.com/brand-radar), you can match a brand as an entity instead of plain text, so “Apple” the company isn’t lumped in with apples the fruit.

Each term can be set to Entity is, Entity contains, or Text, with optional Company or Product filters.

I decided in the end that only name searches should count.

Finally, whatever you do, make the system keep what it rejected, not just what it accepted, along with the reason.

You can see here that the system has already wrongly rejected certain queries that are real questions. That's the process working. So I can now go in and make sure the LLM doesn't do this again.

That rejected list is your early warning system. If a genuine question ever ends up in there, you'll spot it in seconds and fix the rule. If you only see the final output, you'll never know what went missing.

## 5. Make one piece from start to finish

At this point, it’s tempting to automate everything. Don’t.

Always start with one thing first.

For example, I made sure the automation worked perfectly for Top Google Searches before I even thought about expanding it to everything else.

It's tempting to go big. You've done all this prep, the agent seems smart, why not point it at all 12 datasets at once?

There’s a very practical reason for this: You want to catch all its mistakes before anything goes live. And it's a lot easier to catch mistakes in one output than in 12. If all 12 are wrong, you don't even know where to start looking.

Starting small also lets you gradually define what the system is and isn’t allowed to change.

For example, I originally only wanted the tables changed.

Nothing else. Because I was afraid that if I asked the agent to improve the article, it’ll make a mess. Em dashes, AI-isms, and the like.

Once I was satisfied with what it did (and not immediately, over the course of 2-3 months), I then started to allow it to make bigger changes.

For example, the first line in this intro is now “programmatic”, in the sense that it’ll change according to what the top searches are in the table.

Another example: This image also generates each time the table is updated (across all the different posts for the different platforms):

I’ve started playing around with how to improve the tables to have more interesting data and also help the reader:

I also recommend generating an output at every major stage of the workflow.

| Stage | What it does | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fetch | Pulls raw data from each source | Raw data file |
| Clean | Removes irrelevant results | Cleaned list + rejected list |
| Classify | Sorts and labels what's left (e.g., is this a person?) | Classified list |
| Build | Creates the new tables and charts | Tables and charts |
| Update | Writes the changes into the WordPress draft | WordPress draft |
| Notify | Tells me it's done | Email |

This setup has saved me more times than I can count. If there's a mistake, I don't have to restart the whole thing from the top. I check each output, find the stage where things went wrong, fix it, and rerun from there.

Ideally, it should also keep all the data it has changed or updated over time. Mine does. That means I'm building a historical dataset every month. In the future, I can use it to make charts and sparklines that show how searches change over time. That's content nobody else can make, because nobody else has the data.

Finally, the one rule for myself: I never let AI publish automatically for me.

However good the automation gets, we need a human in the loop to keep an eye on things, just in case anything goes wrong. And eventually, something always does.

More than that, someone needs to be responsible for what goes live.

I think of it like being the head chef at a world-class restaurant.

The head chef may not personally cook every single dish anymore. They have sous chefs, line cooks, pastry chefs, and an entire team doing the work.

But everything that leaves the kitchen goes out under their name. If a customer gets a bad plate, it's the head chef's reputation on the line. So they check every dish before it's served.

Your automation is your kitchen. **You're the head chef now.** Nothing should leave without your sign-off.

## 6. Run it for real, then put it on a schedule

Once your one piece works in testing, run the whole thing for real, from start to finish, exactly as it would run on its own.

Then compare the output with your human-made version, side by side. Here's what I'd check:

*   **Numbers:** Spot-check a handful against the source. Are they correct?
*   **Rejections:** Scan the rejected list. Did anything good get thrown out?
*   **Formatting:** Does it match the rest of the article and your house style?
*   **Rewritten text:** If it touched the intro or headings, does it still sound like you?
*   **Links, dates, and small stuff:** The things readers notice immediately when they're wrong.

Keep this question in mind: Would I have published this if I'd made it myself?

When everything looks good, set up a schedule (e.g., monthly).

A couple of things to think about here:

*   **Timing.** Schedule it after your data sources refresh. Otherwise, you'll get a beautifully formatted update of last month's data.
*   **Failure alerts.** Make sure it tells you when something goes wrong, not just when it's done. The worst kind of failure is the silent one, where the automation quietly doesn't run and nobody notices for three months.

## 7. Scale it up

When you're happy with the workflow, it's time to expand it.

That's what I did. Once I was happy with everything coming out of Top Google Searches, I rolled it out across all the other posts I wanted to update, one at a time.

Yes, it takes a while. Each new article has its own quirks. Most Searched People needed completely different rules from Most Expensive Keywords. But remember: it's easier to fix one thing than everything at once. And every article you add gets easier, because most of the pipeline is already built.

But in my case, I didn't just scale up my own workflow. I shared the process with the team, and it inspired them to build things too.

So "scaling it up" doesn't just mean scaling your own processes. It can mean scaling it across your entire department, or even the entire company.

That's how true AI adoption happens. Not by sending a company-wide memo saying "use AI more." That just produces anxiety and a lot of ChatGPT tabs. It happens when someone builds something that works, shows it to their colleagues, and they go: "Wait, can I do that for my thing too?"

## What still goes wrong with my workflow

So is it over once you've set up the automation? Can you finally be in Bali sipping cocktails while AI does all your work?

Unfortunately, no. The last I checked, I’m still in London.

Human review is still necessary. And because AI keeps changing and improving, your automations _will_ break.

If a popular, well-maintained plugin can break overnight, your homemade automation definitely can.

Here’s my own personal example: I built my automation in the same workspace as our content team. Ryan added a new secret or bridge for their own workflows, but unknowingly broke my automation.

Here are the things most likely to go wrong:

*   **Model updates.** A new model version can interpret the same instructions differently. Rules that worked last month might suddenly be ignored, or followed a little too literally.
*   **Source changes.** APIs change, data formats shift, and an export you relied on gets a new column.
*   **Weird data.** A news event can send a random keyword to the top of the charts overnight. Your automation will happily report it unless you've told it to flag unusual spikes.
*   **Rule drift.** The world changes. A new movie comes out with a question for a title, and your rules don't cover it yet.
*   **Formatting breaks.** A CMS update, a theme change, or a new block type, and suddenly your tables look like they were built in 1998.

So you’ll have to keep on maintaining your automations and making sure everything continues to work well.

Again, back to the same restaurant analogy: Even as a chef climbs the ranks, they don't stop checking in on their sous chefs and junior chefs. Recipes get tweaked, suppliers change, new staff join. So they keep tasting, keep checking, and keep correcting, so every dish on the menu comes out perfect.

Same with your automations.

## Final thoughts

I think the least useful way to approach automated content creation is to ask how AI can make as much content as possible.

We already have enough content.

The better question is:

**What parts of making genuinely useful content are stopping us from doing more of it?**

Get AI to handle the boring parts, so you can spend your time on the parts that actually need you: the ideas, the opinions, the experience, the taste. The stuff no model can fake.

That should be the future of working together with AI on content.

Title: How the AI boom might really end: 5 scenarios

URL Source: https://martinalderson.com/posts/how-the-ai-boom-might-really-end/

Published Time: 2026-10-18T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
With the Anthropic IPO gathering pace - and chip stocks just posting their [longest losing streak since 2008](https://ng.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/chip-index-sox-posts-longest-losing-streak-since-2008-as-ai-worries-deepen-2741698) amid [worries about AI debt](https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/16/investing/tech-stocks-ai-coreweave), I thought it'd be worth writing up some of my thoughts I've put together while thinking through what may happen. By no means is this meant to be exhaustive - just a list of what _I_ think is the most interesting to think through.

Before I dive into the scenarios, while I'm sure there are going to be failures and mispricing of asset classes - like any huge investment wave - I think it's worth saying that unlike many bubbles there is an _enormous_ amount of value being created.

In essence, I think this is the first time capital can be turned into intelligence. You buy (or borrow money for) GPUs, you get tokens out which represent a growing share of professional service work. I'm certainly biased as a software engineer by trade - the models just get better and better at coding and it's humbling to see it do my previous tasks _so_ quickly and increasingly _better_ than I can do them.

And unlike (say) the dotcom boom, which was arguably _directionally_ correct, but far too early, we're seeing mass adoption and _huge_ revenues being generated, far quicker than in the late 90s.

So thinking through this, I'd group the scenarios into two categories. Firstly, AI _itself_ doesn't deliver the value promised _or_ gets stopped by external factors. I think these are worth thinking through.

The other category - and potentially more likely - is that AI works well, but the value doesn't flow to the people that are putting the money in. I think this is where the unwinding could happen, and arguably is already showing up.

## Group 1: AI disappoints or gets stopped

### Models stop getting any better

While it's hard to argue that the models as is aren't "good" at specific tasks now, it may well be that we hit a scaling wall. Increasing amounts of capex is pumped into model training, but the results are incrementally better. This leads to a "hard" wall on progress until another architecture or approach potentially comes along.

This one I'd discount for now. We're seeing no signs of progress slowing, and we're seeing very fast advancement in capabilities. And _even_ if this did happen, most organisations and people aren't using anywhere near their full power.

The one watch out though which is a bit more insidious is that the models continue getting better at specific tasks, but start regressing badly in others. I feel Opus 5 was a good example of this - better at coding, but produced infuriatingly hard-to-read prose. Perhaps we'll see models more focused at specific tasks if this gets harder to mitigate (much like the Codex series of GPT models, which then got unified back into the main GPT models).

### Alignment risks

The other _major_ risk with AI is that it ends up doing something _bad_ in the real world. We've already seen the [Hugging Face incident](https://martinalderson.com/posts/huggingface-openai-exploit/) as a 'warning shot'. But there are far more catastrophic risks at play - for example, shutting down national infrastructure, or hacking a major financial institution that results in systemic risk across markets. Or, it goes full Skynet.

There is no doubt this would cause enormous political upheaval that would lead to very rapid and severe backlash. Where the industry goes after that is hard to see - potentially progress gets frozen, resulting in far fewer orders for GPUs. On the other hand, it's hard for me to see a globally coordinated moratorium on AI given the breakneck competition between (primarily) the US and China. If it happened in China, is the US likely to follow suit? Or would it, instead, be blamed on "defective Chinese" models, and the US continues as is? Equally, if it happens in the US, does China pause or see this as a once in a generation opportunity to leap ahead?

I think we are getting dangerously close to an incident that may cause some sort of significant pullback in AI spending. It's certainly hard to predict, and the severity matters a lot - along with human impact.

### Datacentre ban

Slightly less science fiction-y would be widespread local or political opposition to datacentre rollouts causing a very widespread pause on new capacity coming on stream.

While this is certainly happening - I have a suspicion this could be one of the key battlelines for the 2028 US election cycle - it again would have to be a global ban to have any significant effect. If the US does a ban, projects and investments would quickly shift to other jurisdictions.

And I'm almost certain that China would not even entertain any sort of ban like this, which again adds a geopolitical angle to it. Would the US really want to go ahead with a national ban when China _already_ has a commanding lead in electricity capacity (if not semiconductors).

As such, I can't see this having a great effect on the deployment as a whole. The _real_ weakness lies in financing these deals. Much like Ørsted needed a [$9.4bn rights issue](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/02/09/revolution-wind-developer-records-10m-q4-impairment-from-trump-suspension-order/) after US stop-work orders on its offshore wind projects spooked its financing, we could quickly see a domino effect of financing failures caused by it.

## Group 2: AI works, but the capex holders don't capture the value

### Open weights get so good they collapse margins

I think this is the standout from where I see the risk and something I've been writing about for a while now. We're in the middle of a _brutal_ inference price war - if you want to read more read my [other recent article](https://martinalderson.com/posts/ai-margin-collapse-gathering-pace/).

This is largely caused by open weights models crossing the threshold of being "good enough" for many tasks.

Anthropic releasing Haiku 5.5 at a huge discount - 90% cheaper on short context windows - means that for shorter, bulk tasks, Anthropic & OpenAI are actually as cheap as, or _cheaper_ than, comparable open weights models. This doesn't apply for longer agentic tasks with Haiku - the price jumps 5x once you go over 100K tokens of context. Interestingly, OpenAI is far more aggressive here: GPT-6 Luna only goes up 1.5-2x, and only past 272K tokens. But I was surprised recently to find that no reputable inference provider offers comparable open weights models (e.g. DeepSeek) at any significant discount to Haiku and Luna, which is an enormous change from where we were at the start of the year, where the frontier labs were charging 10-20x more than open weight models.

How much this cannibalises their more expensive models is up for debate. They've done the pricing in such a way that for longer agentic tasks, open weight models are still very attractive.

But the perpetual price drops must be having some impact on margins, even if it does lead to them (re)taking market share from open weights competitors.

So the _hope_ is that they continue cutting prices, but revenue/token growth outstrips that. It is certainly possible - but it shows how fast this market switches that we've now got frontier labs offering this inference _at all_.

The wildcard I would keep though is that while the open weights labs have kept pace, we can't rule out the frontier labs' ability to throw a _lot_ of compute and brainpower at new models. Opus 5.5, for example, is an excellent model for more demanding tasks. And the Chinese labs are clearly short of hardware _and_ facing [new export restrictions](https://fortune.com/2026/10/16/china-restrictions-ai-chips-solar-power-exports-security/) from the Chinese government.

### Huge efficiency breakthroughs

Note that the previous scenario, while catastrophic for the frontier labs if this compression continues, arguably _increases_ demand for semiconductors, memory and the related supply chain.

But another risk is that if there are huge efficiency breakthroughs, either through hardware _or_ software/model improvements. This is what killed the [telecoms boom in the early 2000s](https://martinalderson.com/posts/are-we-really-repeating-the-telecoms-crash-with-ai-datacenters/) - it wasn't so much that bandwidth growth stopped, but the efficiency of fibre optics far outpaced the demands.

So far we've seen _a lot_ of innovation on the model side, but hardware has struggled to keep pace. Discounting all the hype stats that Nvidia etc put out for each new generation[[1]](https://martinalderson.com/posts/how-the-ai-boom-might-really-end/#fn1), underlying tokens/watt - the best figure to watch - is improving far slower than the headlines suggest.

The model efficiency improvements have been pretty amazing to watch. But so far, this has all been put into longer context windows (enabling longer running agentic tasks) and have enabled some of the price decreases we've seen.

But, there is a world where a new hardware or software approach does lead, much like DWDM fibre back in the 2000s, to efficiency running far, far ahead of token growth, even taking Jevons paradox into account.

My gut says that token demand is growing so fast, and will _continue_ to grow so fast that it will consume all efficiency gains in the near future. The key way to track this I think is _not_ looking at some of the "token cost indexes" that get posted about - this doesn't adjust for the exponential growth in demand - but instead look at the cost of GPUs on the spot market. If we start seeing _big_, _broad_ drops across all compute types, then that's a clear sign that supply and demand is starting to reach equilibrium and this scenario is starting to play out.

## Conclusion

There are no doubt many risks to the AI "economy", and it's always easy to point to whatever one is making the most news.

But to me the _real_ question is whether AI progress is turning into tangible value. Right now - for me, and many others, the answer is a resounding yes. Token consumption is going through the roof, because as models get better more and more tasks can be executed with AI. And I still think early adopters that are pushing agentic workflows comprise a small single-digit percentage of the professional services market as a whole.

But this doesn't mean that the labs making and serving those models take the benefit. History is littered with huge technological advancements which went to _consumer surplus_, not whoever bet the most capital.

And my view is that's what we are seeing right now. The frontier labs are in serious peril of losing margin, and therefore market valuation, to open weights competitors.

The important point though is that the frontier labs do not make up the whole market. Tokens need compute, memory and power whether it's a frontier lab or open weights.

I see endless analysis of OpenAI vs Anthropic revenue figures. What's far _more_ important to the AI ecosystem is _overall_ revenues. And as the market continues to fragment, it's harder and harder to join that together. Unless AI does hit a wall, open weights may mean the end of the boom in frontier labs valuations. But the underlying supply chains may be doing _better_ than ever.

Which is why I think the market has this week backwards. Chip stocks are being punished just as TSMC reports record revenue and says [AI demand still exceeds supply](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/10/15/tsmc-tsm-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/).

The one caveat is leverage. So much of this buildout is debt-funded that even small changes can unwind far faster, and far more completely, than they should. CoreWeave's [credit default swaps hit distressed levels](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/15/coreweave-credit-default-swaps-hit-distress-levels-as-investors-sour-on-ai-debt.html) this week on a hot inflation print and a [viral chart](https://fortune.com/2026/10/16/coreweave-investor-explains-ai-neocloud-debt/) - not because anyone stopped wanting GPUs.

If the AI boom ends, I don't think it ends with fewer tokens. It ends with the same tokens - or far more - flowing to far more people at far lower margins.

* * *

1.   Nvidia's headline generation-on-generation numbers mostly come from dropping precision (FP8 to FP4), not from the silicon getting more efficient. Halving precision roughly doubles throughput on the same hardware, but you're trading accuracy for speed, and most production inference still runs at FP8 or BF16. Compare like-for-like at FP8 and H100 to Vera Rubin is roughly 2.7x per watt over three generations - about 1.5x a generation. Over the same period power per GPU went from ~700W to ~2,300W, so more than half the per-GPU gain is simply drawing more power through bigger, multi-die packages. Moore's law is slowing, and there's a hard limit to how far you can cut precision. Once both run out, the tok/watt gains have to come from somewhere else. Title: What on earth is going on with AI pricing and packaging?

URL Source: https://www.elenaverna.com/p/what-on-earth-is-going-on-with-ai

Published Time: 2026-10-16T14:22:50+00:00

Markdown Content:
I recently went down a rabbit hole looking at AI pricing pages, trying to answer what I thought was a pretty basic question: If I pay $20 a month for an AI product, what exactly am I getting? How much can I use it? And how do I know if I need the $20 plan, the $100 plan, or the “contact sales and surrender your firstborn” plan?

I’ve spent an embarrassing amount of my career obsessing over pricing and packaging and most importantly I work for an AI company, so I assumed I could figure this out. Turns out, I have vastly overestimated my qualifications.

Some companies promise 5x more usage without explaining 5x of WHAT. Others give you hundreds of millions of tokens, which sounds generous until you realize you have no idea what a token buys you. Some have decided that having a pricing page is optional.

Just imagine interviewing someone who tells you they’ll cost 500 million tokens a week, or that for twice the salary they’ll do “5x more work,” without telling you how much work they do today. Funny, right? In AI, we call that a pricing page.

And here’s the fascinating part: these companies are WILDLY successful. Millions of users, eye-watering valuations, explosive growth. Apparently, understanding what you’re paying for is no longer a prerequisite for buying software.

Before anyone accuses me of throwing stones from my very glass house, I lead growth at Lovable, and we have the same problem. We sell credits for a product that can build websites, apps, internal tools, presentations, and whatever else someone dreams up tomorrow. Good luck wrapping that into three subscription tiers.

But maybe we’re not all just terrible at pricing. AI products can do almost anything, and the cost of doing it can vary wildly. Unlike traditional SaaS, where we could reasonably charge for seats, storage, or transactions, we’re now trying to price work that neither the customer nor the company can reliably predict.

So far, the industry is getting away with it because the products are just that good and new and exciting. But will that last? Early adopters will tolerate mystery credits and surprise usage limits. The mass market? I’m less convinced.

Let’s examine a few:

_(This is a full circle moment for me because I started my career at SurveyMonkey! Will always be rooting for them :))_

One of the very hyped products out there right now, giving all kinds of people all kinds of agents. So, how do they do pricing?

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yfJi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F804ad6f5-8e1d-445d-845c-c3387691cc51_1994x2048.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yfJi!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F804ad6f5-8e1d-445d-845c-c3387691cc51_1994x2048.png)

This starts out pretty simple - 4 plans. Easy! But… what’s the actual amount of AI usage are you getting? Grok has somehow built an entire pricing strategy around multiplying a number they refuse to tell you.

Premium gets 4x more usage than Plus. Super gets 15x more. Except nowhere does it explain how much usage Plus actually includes. So we’re multiplying an unknown number by increasingly impressive numbers and calling it pricing.

Muse is on fire right now and has a pretty amusing approach to pricing: just don’t have a pricing page in logged out state at all. I searched everywhere and the closest thing I found was a Facebook Answers post. Apparently, pricing is now a community-sourced mystery.

They do have pricing in-app: $20/month for 500 MILLION tokens per week.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YXbM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe6e0849d-47ed-484f-b5cd-eafc467eab18_1320x1537.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YXbM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe6e0849d-47ed-484f-b5cd-eafc467eab18_1320x1537.jpeg)

Half a billion! Of something! I have no idea what that buys me, but I’m pretty sure I’m supposed to be impressed.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Wvga!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2f054187-430c-42a4-a24a-07ca70217077_500x500.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Wvga!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2f054187-430c-42a4-a24a-07ca70217077_500x500.png)

P.S. Extra credit for charging on monthly frequency, but giving tokens on the weekly basis.

I’m not sparing my own company either… we have this issue, too:

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3DIv!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9474e0f7-a1a9-44d9-b03c-827213fd8235_2048x1270.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3DIv!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9474e0f7-a1a9-44d9-b03c-827213fd8235_2048x1270.png)

So, we give you credits… but what does that mean? $25/mo gives you 100 Pro credits, but no one knows what that means until you start building and see it for yourself. I’d love nothing more than to tie our pricing to outcomes, whether that’s hosting, a take rate on GMV (hi, Shopify!), or something else entirely. But ideally, we’d still be in business by the time you get there (and right now we wouldn’t).

So hot right now. This is their site.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!p4un!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2438f293-e3cc-48ed-ba62-743016fd6452_2048x1427.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!p4un!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2438f293-e3cc-48ed-ba62-743016fd6452_2048x1427.png)

Which brings us to the fact that if your AI product is awesome right now, you don’t need pricing figured out to get a ton of users. You don’t even need a proper marketing website. You can just launch, go viral, and worry about all those pesky things we used to consider prerequisites for running a legitimate company later. What a time to be alive. Anyway, moving on.

Their pricing is similar to Lovable’s: credits! Except they give you WAY more of them. Because why give someone 100 imaginary dollars when you can give them 10,000? Welcome to arcade economics, where the money is made up and the numbers are designed to impress.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!b3PT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9d5a9acc-1390-4132-806b-c5a0cd1b33d2_2048x1773.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!b3PT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9d5a9acc-1390-4132-806b-c5a0cd1b33d2_2048x1773.png)

But wait.. there is more! a LOT more.

It is flexible alright. Human brain is not evolved enough to be able to comprehend this many plan options and decision making dimensions.

Now let’s talk about what the big boys and girls are up to:

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XRVg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa61ae6d9-452b-42fe-8fa9-1fa35fd38d9d_2048x1461.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XRVg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa61ae6d9-452b-42fe-8fa9-1fa35fd38d9d_2048x1461.png)

Four plans for individuals. The Free plan’s feature list is basically just “Limited” copy-pasted all the way down. The first paid plan (‘Go’) offers a highly quantitative increase of ‘More’ across 4 of the elements.

The Plus and Pro plans pretty much just choose a different adjective and copy-paste down the line: Either taking your ‘Limited’ or ‘More’ access and then leveling it up to ‘Expanded’ or ‘Maximum.’

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wThX!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f4df708-d503-4d14-94ba-a948ec761a16_612x408.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wThX!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f4df708-d503-4d14-94ba-a948ec761a16_612x408.png)

Perhaps it’s more clear from their frenemies over at Anthropic?

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3CtV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1464fb9f-435a-491f-ae78-5f79141c6f17_2048x1624.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3CtV!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1464fb9f-435a-491f-ae78-5f79141c6f17_2048x1624.png)

At least the Free tier isn’t so blatantly framed as a second-class citizen. But… yeah, when I pay for Pro I get… ‘More usage’! More than… what? There’s that helpful little * there… that doesn’t actually connect to anything below. And Max is 5x or 20x more usage. That sure is a lot more than whatever it’s a lot more than!

I think there are four things happening simultaneously, and they’re making an already complicated problem considerably worse.

Let’s start with something we’ve been doing in pricing for decades: making money feel less like money. There’s a concept in behavioral economics called mental accounting, which helps explain why people treat different forms of money differently. It’s why casinos have chips, arcades have tokens, and every other mobile game seems to have its own imaginary currency that somehow requires you to buy 1,200 gems to purchase something that costs 950.

AI companies have enthusiastically adopted this approach. Instead of dollars, we give people credits, tokens, compute units, and whatever other imaginary currency our pricing teams come up with. And yes, these currencies can make it harder to understand what you’re actually spending. When you’re using 12 credits instead of $3, you might be less inclined to think about the real cost.

But here’s where I have to defend the industry, including Lovable. Credits aren’t necessarily a sinister monetization scheme. They can solve a real problem. When your product has multiple AI models, tools, and actions that each have different underlying costs, a common currency makes it possible to package them into something resembling a subscription. Otherwise, we’d essentially be asking customers to manage a miniature AWS bill every time they wanted to accomplish something.

The problem isn’t necessarily that we invented these currencies. It’s that we’ve done a bad job explaining what they’re worth. If I give someone 100 Lovable credits, I should be able to help them understand roughly what they can accomplish with them. Otherwise, I’m not really selling them 100 units of value. I’m selling them 100 units of mystery. But this is incredibly hard when you have AI doing something custom for every customer!

Once you invent a currency, you can make the numbers as big as you want. Why give someone 100 credits when you could give them 10,000? Or 500 million tokens? Bigger numbers create an impression of generosity :)

And notice how much of AI pricing is framed around quantities rather than value. More tokens. More credits. Maximum messages. Extended access.

Nobody wakes up wanting 500 million tokens (sorry Muse). They wake up wanting to get something done. But we have no idea what our products can even do for our customers, since AI leaves it so open ended. So we are stuck once again.

This is where the problem gets genuinely interesting. Traditional SaaS had its own pricing problems, but at least we generally had some reasonably understandable ways to measure consumption. You could charge per seat, per transaction, per gigabyte of storage, or per API call. These weren’t perfect measures of customer value, but they were usually predictable enough that someone could estimate what they needed before buying.

AI has made that considerably more complicated. What exactly is the unit of consumption for an agent that can research your competitors, create a marketing campaign, build an application, or handle your customer support? Is it the number of messages you send? The number of tasks it completes? The time it spends working? The number of times it calls another tool? And more importantly, which of those measurements would actually make sense to the customer?

Some products have it easier. ElevenLabs can charge by minutes of generated audio or agent calls. Firecrawl can translate credits into pages scraped or searches performed. Those units aren’t perfect, but at least they’re connected to something a customer can imagine needing.

But the more general-purpose the product becomes, the harder this gets. An agent that can do almost anything doesn’t have one obvious unit of value. If we charge by the hour, customers might wonder why they’re paying more for a slow agent. If we charge by the task, how do we distinguish between answering an email and building an entire application? And if we charge for successful outcomes, who decides what success means?

The irony is that we’re building increasingly sophisticated AI systems capable of doing work we couldn’t have imagined automating a few years ago, and then asking customers to estimate how many tokens they’ll need to use them.

It’s like selling someone a car and asking them to estimate how many times the engine will fire… whut.

And here’s the part that makes this genuinely difficult for AI companies. We aren’t just struggling to predict what customers will do with our products. We’re also struggling to predict what those actions will cost us.

In traditional SaaS, serving another customer wasn’t free, but the marginal cost was often relatively low and predictable. You could offer a subscription with generous usage allowances and have a pretty reasonable idea of the economics. AI changes that equation because every additional interaction can carry a meaningful inference cost, and different interactions can consume vastly different amounts of resources. (This goes away if LLMs become basically free… but we are not there yet).

This is especially challenging with agents, because they’re not just responding to a single request. They can plan, execute multiple steps, call tools, make mistakes, retry, and decide that the task requires a completely different approach. Two customers might ask for essentially the same outcome, but the underlying work (and cost) could be dramatically different.

(P.S. And then there’s also FRAUD. Bots, stolen accounts, and people abusing free tiers. In traditional SaaS, a fake signup mostly messed up your conversion metrics. In AI, it ruins your bottom line. So now we have to predict not just what customers will use, but how creatively people will try to bankrupt us. Fun times!)

This is why I think the answer isn’t as simple as “just charge for outcomes.” I love outcome-based pricing in theory. It aligns the company’s success with the customer’s success, which is what pricing should ideally do. But it’s considerably harder to implement when the same outcome can have wildly different delivery costs, when outcomes are difficult to define, or when the customer and the AI company disagree about whether the job was successfully completed.

I don’t have a magical answer to AI pricing, which is somewhat disappointing given how many years I’ve spent thinking about monetization. But I do think this is going to become one of the most important problems AI companies need to solve as the technology moves beyond early adopters.

Right now, we’re surrounded by people who are willing to tolerate a ridiculous amount of complexity to use these products (Hi there, you AI pioneer! Yes, I’m talking to YOU). They’ll compare tokens, look up credit consumption, calculate model costs, and accept that their usage limits might change tomorrow. But those people aren’t the entire market. They’re the people who are enthusiastic enough about AI to put up with things most customers would find completely unacceptable.

If we want AI to reach a much broader audience, we can’t expect everyone to become an expert in inference economics just to figure out which subscription to buy. We have to make the cost of accomplishing something understandable, reasonably predictable, and within the customer’s control.

I think whoever figures this out first will have a massive competitive advantage. Not necessarily the company with the cheapest AI, the smartest model, or the most generous allocation of imaginary credits. But the company that can make AI pricing understandable, predictable, and aligned with customer value, without bankrupting itself in the process.

We’ve spent the last few years racing to make AI more powerful. The next big race might just be figuring out how to charge for it. And honestly, I’m not sure which is harder.

_Edited by [Jonathan Yagel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jwbyagel/)._

[OpenAI](https://cryptobriefing.com/markets/openai/) wants ChatGPT to be the place where people ask questions and, increasingly, where brands answer them. Early advertisers are finding the second half of that plan harder than it looks.

Results from the ChatGPT advertising pilot are all over the map. Some marketers say their acquisition costs beat search, while others say they are paying for clicks that never become a sale.

The recurring complaint is targeting. Ads are not consistently reaching the right users at the right point in a conversation, and that gap is showing up in the conversion numbers.

## The numbers behind the mixed reviews

As of late 2026, ads appear on approximately 25.94% of commercial prompts. Those are queries with some kind of buying or shopping angle, which is the territory advertisers care about most.

Around 14% of ads have limited or no connection to the user’s query or the conversation thread.

Ad impressions also often reach users who show no clear purchase intent. Someone researching a topic out of curiosity is not the same as someone ready to buy, and the platform does not always tell the difference.

Click-through rates have landed between 0.5% and 2%. Cost-per-click ranges from under $3 to over $10, a spread wide enough that two advertisers could have very different experiences on the same platform.

One advertiser spent $477 over six weeks, collected 370 clicks, and recorded zero conversions.

Outcomes like that have pushed some marketers to treat ChatGPT ads as an experiment rather than a core channel. In practice, that usually means a small test budget, close monitoring, and little appetite for scaling until the data improves.

## The case for patience

The picture is not uniformly grim. Some advertisers, particularly those working through partnerships, have posted competitive cost-per-acquisition figures.

For certain partners, CPA was reported to be 15.3% lower than paid search benchmarks.

OpenAI claims a 112% improvement in click-through rates over one tracking period. The company has also rolled out improved measurement tools and new creative formats in response to advertiser feedback.

The platform reached a claimed $1 billion annualized revenue run rate in under 200 days of launch.

## Why conversational ads are a different animal

OpenAI launched the pilot in early 2026 with an ambitious goal: rethinking how ads get delivered inside conversation-based AI. That is a different problem from placing an ad next to a search result.

The 14% figure for loosely connected or unrelated ads is the clearest sign of that difficulty. When nearly one in seven ads misses the conversation, users learn to tune them out, and low click-through rates follow.

## What this means for advertisers and OpenAI

There are a few signals worth watching. The first is whether the share of irrelevant or loosely connected ads falls from around 14%, since relevance sits upstream of nearly every other metric.

The second is whether OpenAI’s claimed improvement in click-through rates carries through to conversions. More clicks only matter if some of them turn into customers.

The third is whether results from partnership deals, where CPA has looked competitive, start to show up for ordinary self-serve advertisers. If the strong numbers stay concentrated among a handful of partners, the platform will look less like a new advertising channel and more like a set of custom arrangements.

Title: Bots Used to Be a Threat. Now They’re Your Customers.

URL Source: https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/tech/bots-used-to-be-a-threat-now-theyre-your-customers

Published Time: 2026-10-16T12:30:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Listen to this post

For the last thirty years, digital marketers have been focused on keeping bots out. The very term “bots” had a negative connotation, and the layers and layers of protection we’ve built are now a liability to brands’ web stacks.

This isn’t because security stopped mattering… It hasn’t. But all of the CAPTCHAs, rate limits, login walls, fingerprinting and internet fortresses we’ve tried to build must be re-examined in the modern context of AI. Brands may be doing themselves a disservice with the default position that automated traffic is hostile until proven otherwise.

My co-founder has been preaching about this for years, and I’ve nodded along for most of them. Only recently have I felt the upside-downness of it, and how much of what we built to protect brands now works against us.

## **Understanding the scale of the problem**

Bots are [now](https://www.imperva.com/blog/bad-bot-report-2026-bots-agentic-age/) 53% of web traffic — that’s the stat everyone repeats on LinkedIn. Although if you double-click, the context is even more important since agents are doing way more than they used to. Often, they don’t just scan sites; they interact and execute workflows, which makes good and [bad traffic](https://www.entrepreneur.com/science-technology/the-impact-of-bad-bots-can-be-devastating-for-your/445121?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=1ceb0cc1b7c988b8517906c97c6fb1ad&itm_source=smart-linking "The Impact of Bad Bots Can Be Devastating for Your Business. Here’s How.") harder to tell apart.

That is where the problem lies and what we need to solve for — Your defenses can’t tell the difference between someone scraping your catalog nefariously and someone’s assistant trying to buy from it. Same door, same knock. It is hard to distinguish between bots working on behalf of a company, agents working for a consumer, and [bad actors](https://www.entrepreneur.com/science-technology/this-strategy-will-help-you-battle-bots-in-retail-and/428893?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=abffb27d6531e01f4ea9f7274ee9c8ed&itm_source=smart-linking "How to Solve ‘Botting’ Problems in Retail and E-Commerce") (who are still bad actors).​

## Brands are starting to adopt new strategies

As agents act more and more on behalf of consumers, websites begin to hold a very different spot in the customer journey. A customer tells their assistant: “Find me trail runners, men’s size 10.5, waterproof, under $150, at my door by Saturday.” That agent lands on your site and starts guessing. It reads your page code, infers what your buttons do, and clicks.

Now think about what happens when it doesn’t work or it can’t get proper access. The agent doesn’t email support or try again tomorrow. It moves to a site that was easier to operate and tells your customer it found the shoes there. No cart, no session, no signal anything happened.

That’s the shift marketers should feel in their chest. Site friction used to cost you conversion rate. Now it costs you the consideration set, silently, before a number lands in your analytics.

Instead of the agent reverse-engineering your site, brands need to adopt new protocols and site structures that are helpful, not defensive of bots.​ The risk is that skipping this means agents may route around you to marketplaces and resellers where the data is easy to get. Your product becomes a row in somebody else’s comparison table. No brand story, no bundle, no reason to pick you over the line below except price and a star.​​

Bots must be considered a [first-class audience](https://www.entrepreneur.com/leadership/why-ai-is-forcing-a-rethink-of-business-metrics/502125?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=4a89ef957e48098a15c4c25deb4002d8&itm_source=smart-linking "We’re Measuring AI Agents Like Humans — and It’s Breaking Our Businesses") when optimizing your website and digital experience. Here are a few things that brands need to consider as they evolve their web experiences for both human consumers & bots.

## 1. Find out what you’re blocking and make it easier for “good bots” to consume your site

Your bot policy likely got set by a vendor default at some point and often nobody has opened it since. There’s a real chance you’re blocking some of your own demand and calling it protection. ​

Example: Plenty of brands still block important buts like [ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity](https://www.entrepreneur.com/building-a-business/ai-is-changing-how-businesses-are-found-online-thats-why-you-need-to-rebuild-your-search-strategy?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=73ad192ee79eebbcf007b10b130a465b&itm_source=smart-linking "AI Is Changing How Businesses Are Found Online. That’s Why You Need to Rebuild Your Search Strategy.") use to fetch pages when someone asks a question. If those bots can’t reach your site, you [can’t be cited](https://www.entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/how-smart-founders-are-adapting-to-the-zero-click-economy/502221?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=d6a4069e2d45f2ee4d966719dab53a9f&itm_source=smart-linking "The Zero-Click Economy Is Here, and It’s Stealing the Traffic You Rely On. Here’s How to Adapt Before It’s Too Late.") when a shopper asks [AI what to buy](https://www.entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/the-way-people-shop-has-quietly-changed-forever-and/503736?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=3c916b683f7086e005e868885152cad1&itm_source=smart-linking "The Way People Shop Has Quietly Changed Forever — and Only Brands That Adapt Will Lead the Next Trillion-Dollar Market").

## 2. Make sure that your site structure is laid out well for agents, and not just well styled

Structure beats styling when it comes to agents. Structuring data such as pricing, availability/inventory, FAQs, sizing, shipping windows, return policy, etc. is incredibly important.

​Example: Having Ratings & Reviews data live a well designed carousel or an image, means they don’t exist to agents.

## 3. Map your customer journey and make sure the actions agents need to take are well articulated

Start by identifying the key things a customer would want an agent to do on your site and optimize specifically for those.

Example: A footwear brand would want to make sure agents can easily navigate to buy their products, read reviews, and compare to their main competitors. Given these are all steps in journey an agent is likely to take on behalf of a shopper, brands must re-engineer parts of their website to make these steps seamless not just for human shoppers but agents too.

## 4. Revamp your analytics stack

Often an agent visits your site and reports back to the consumer on a different surface than your website. Ultimately, what matters is whether you showed up, got cited, and got picked within the AI Search interaction between AI and your customer. But it also means your web analytics are not a trustworthy source of truth when agents are the ones visiting it, and then taking the data and experience onto new surfaces not mapped by your web analytics.

​Example: Your organic search traffic may have dropped 35% over the past few quarters, but that does not necessarily mean you have gotten 35% less organic impressions. It’s likely that the impressions have just moved from your website (between you and your shopper), and are now taking place across large language models (between an agent and your shopper). For many brands this means a [new set of metrics](https://www.entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/the-ai-search-opportunity-most-companies-are-missing/504202?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=1eafe834739d950d9e7227b265f54a86&itm_source=smart-linking "AI Search Is Growing — But Most Companies Aren’t Tracking It. Here’s How to Turn That Gap Into a Real Advantage.") and analytics are required to understand how bots and AI are changing organic discovery. ​

## Conclusion

None of this means the last thirty years were a mistake. The gates were correct for the internet we had. They’re just pointed at the wrong thing now.

It’s also important to acknowledge that evolving for an agentic internet isn’t just an SEO tweak or checklist to work through. It’s architectural, and marketing owns more of it than marketing expects. Nobody from security is going to walk into your Monday standup and tell you the bot rules are costing you customers.
